Humanoid robots are suddenly getting very fast

The second World Humanoid Robot Games opened Aug. 22 at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, known as the Ice Ribbon, and ran through Aug. 26. Organizers registered 666 teams and 2,056 robots for this year's event. The competition included 51 events and 1,301 competition sessions.
The robots compete in track and field events along with challenges designed around real-world jobs. Organizers have also added tests involving physical skills such as weightlifting and tug of war.

That mix tells you something about what China wants these machines to become. The Games give developers a place to push speed and strength. They also expose weaknesses that can be harder to see in a carefully edited demonstration video.
TianGong Ultra ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds, then 9.32

The first number that grabbed worldwide attention was 9.39 seconds. That was already quicker than Bolt's 9.58-second human record from 2009. The comparison spread fast because almost everyone understands what a 100-meter sprint represents. Then X-Humanoid released its updated results.

The company says TianGong Ultra eventually reached 9.32 seconds, while other X-Humanoid teams recorded times of 9.34, 9.38 and 9.39 seconds. The exact comparison with Bolt needs context. These robots do not start, run or stop under the same conditions as human Olympic athletes.

A Tiangong Ultra humanoid robot crosses the finish line in 8.86 seconds next to Honor humanoid robots during a 100-meter large-size group semifinal race at the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on Aug. 25, 2026. (REUTERS)

However, that does not make the improvement meaningless. A humanoid staying upright at that speed requires serious coordination between its motors, balance system, sensors and software. All of those pieces have to work together while the machine continuously adjusts its body. That is what catches my attention.
Last year's winner took more than twice as long
The rate of improvement becomes even clearer when you look back only one year. At the inaugural World Humanoid Robot Games in 2025, the winning 100-meter robot finished in 21.50 seconds.

Now robots from the same development ecosystem are running the distance in less than 10 seconds. That is an enormous leap in a short period. We have already been following this acceleration at CyberGuy. Earlier this year, we showed you a Chinese humanoid called Bolt that reached 22 mph during testing. Running fast looks impressive on video. Yet the technology underneath that speed could become useful in places far removed from a racetrack.
A robot also jumped about 9 feet 5 inches

Running was only part of the show. An X-Humanoid robot reached 2.88 meters, or about 9 feet 5 inches, in a standing high jump. That height exceeds the recognized men's high jump world record of 2.45 meters, or about 8 feet, set by Cuba's Javier Sotomayor in 1993. Again, we need context.

Sotomayor's world record came from a conventional high jump with a running approach. The robot competed in a standing high jump. Those events use very different mechanics. So the robot did not erase Sotomayor from the record books. What it did demonstrate was impressive explosive power and body control from a humanoid machine. Those capabilities could eventually translate into something far more useful than clearing a bar.
ROBOT LEARNS TO DISMANTLE BROKEN MACHINES
Once robots can move like this, you start asking where they can go

A fast humanoid robot does not need to become a track star to become valuable. Better mobility could help a robot move through a disaster area where sending a person could be dangerous. A machine that stays balanced while carrying equipment could eventually handle physically demanding jobs. Then you start thinking about environments where people would rather avoid going altogether.

Maintenance team members check on Tiangong Ultra humanoid robots after they fall following the 100m large-size group final race at the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games at the National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on Aug. 26, 2026. (REUTERS)
That brings us to the part of this story that deserves much more attention. One developer at the Games believes humanoid robot soldiers could arrive within the next decade.
One developer predicts robot soldiers within 5 to 10 years

Robotics engineer Yang Kun, who works for Shanghai-based humanoid robotics company AG BOT, says that he believes Chinese companies could be only five to 10 years away from robot soldiers. His company's A3 humanoid competed in kickboxing at the Games. Yang described military and combat use as part of where he believes humanoid robotics could eventually go. That prediction deserves context. This comes from one developer. It does not represent an announced Chinese government timetable for deploying humanoid soldiers. I would not take five to 10 years as gospel.

Technology forecasts can move quickly in either direction. A machine can perform beautifully in a controlled environment and then struggle once the surroundings become unpredictable. What I would pay attention to is where developers believe this technology is headed. When people building these machines start discussing military applications, that tells us the conversation has already moved far beyond robots entertaining crowds at sporting events.
A battlefield would expose everything robots still struggle with

Running fast in a straight line is one challenge. Navigating a damaged building while carrying equipment presents an entirely different problem. A robot may encounter unstable ground, blocked paths and people moving unpredictably around it. Then comes the far harder issue of decision-making. A sprint gives a robot a clear destination. Real life rarely does. Military environments make that problem even tougher because communication can disappear without warning. Sensors can misread a situation. Software may face circumstances developers never anticipated.

That is why I would keep some perspective when watching these record-setting performances. The robots are getting impressive. They also still fall down. At the Games, some fast-running robots had trouble stopping after crossing the finish line and crashed into padded barriers. That creates a pretty good visual reminder of the gap between raw speed and reliable control.
China is testing robots for real-world jobs too

The organizers appear very aware of that gap. This year, Beijing upgraded the 100-meter event so robots must compete fully autonomously. Scenario-based events also encourage autonomous positioning, recognition and operation. The robots also face tasks inside settings modeled after factories, hotels and homes. Emergency-response challenges push them into situations where they must interact with their surroundings for longer periods.

That part interests me even more than a sprint record. A robot that runs 100 meters in nine seconds creates a great headline. A robot that can reliably work for hours without somebody constantly guiding it could change entire industries. China appears focused on both. CyberGuy has also reported on efforts to scale humanoid manufacturing in China, with factories preparing to build thousands of machines. That brings us to the larger technology race.
UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES
The U.S.-China tech race now has arms and legs

We hear constantly about competition between the United States and China over artificial intelligence. Humanoid robotics adds a physical layer to that race. The country that develops powerful artificial intelligence gains one advantage. The country that can put that intelligence inside a reliable robot body and manufacture those machines at scale could gain something much larger. Suddenly, the software can move through the physical world. It can enter an industrial facility. It can cross dangerous terrain or potentially operate where sending people would carry significant risk. U.S. regulators are already treating advanced foreign robotics as a national-security concern.

On July 28, the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to its Covered List. The category includes qualifying humanoid robots and other advanced mobile robotic systems. The change means covered new devices generally cannot receive the FCC equipment authorization required for import or sale in the United States unless they receive an applicable conditional approval. That tells you Washington sees connected robots as more than another gadget category.
The AI brain could become the bigger story

For years, humanoid developers faced a frustrating mechanical challenge. How do you make a two-legged machine move efficiently without constantly falling over? Engineers still have plenty of work ahead. Yet today's machines move very differently from the awkward humanoids we watched only a few years ago. That changes what developers can focus on next.

As robot bodies become faster and stronger, artificial intelligence continues improving at the same time. A more capable body could perform difficult physical work. Better AI could help that machine understand what it sees and determine what to do next. Put those advances together and humanoids become much more interesting. We recently showed you another humanoid demonstrating impressive running and movement skills. The biggest hurdle now may become less about making a robot move and more about making sure it makes good decisions once it gets there.
What this means to you

You probably will not see a humanoid robot soldier walking down your street anytime soon. You may encounter the technology behind these machines much sooner. The balance system that keeps a robot upright during a sprint could help one move through rubble after an earthquake. More capable sensors could allow robots to operate around human workers more safely. Factories will likely remain one of the first major targets.

Most buildings and workplaces were designed around the human body. That makes humanoids appealing because companies could potentially deploy them without rebuilding every workspace around a specialized machine. As reliability improves and costs come down, those capabilities could expand into other areas. The military discussion raises much harder questions.

How much decision-making authority should an autonomous machine have? Who carries responsibility if an AI-controlled robot makes a dangerous mistake? Those conversations should happen before the machines become capable enough to force them. Because the technology is moving quickly.
Kurt's key takeaways

The Bolt comparison grabs your attention, but the bigger story for me is how quickly humanoid robots are becoming more capable. A 9.39-second 100-meter run shows how fast the motors, balance systems and software are improving. The military angle deserves attention too. One Chinese robotics engineer predicts robot soldiers could arrive within five to 10 years. I would not treat that timeline as gospel, but it shows where some developers believe this technology is headed. For America, this is another front in the technology race with China. A country that can combine advanced AI with reliable robot bodies and produce large numbers of them could gain a major advantage. We also need perspective. Running fast on a controlled track is far easier than navigating an unpredictable environment and making safe decisions. What I am watching now is how quickly these stronger robot bodies advance alongside increasingly capable AI.

If humanoid robots can outrun us, carry heavy equipment and make more decisions on their own, where would you draw the line on how much power we should give them? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: What is a Tuey-Rodriguez charge? Judge gives instruction to deadlocked Lindsay Clancy jury
summary: The judge in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial issued a rare Tuey-Rodriguez charge after jurors again said they were deadlocked. Learn what the Massachusetts jury instruction is.
story: Fox News correspondent Nate Foy and criminal defense attorney Josh Ritter discuss the deadlocked jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial and the arrest of a woman accused of photographing jurors on ‘The Faulkner Focus.’

A Massachusetts judge overseeing the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy gave jurors a Tuey-Rodriguez charge Wednesday after they reported for a second time that they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict.
The instruction is given to a deadlocked jury to encourage continued deliberations while reminding jurors they should not abandon honestly held beliefs simply to reach a verdict.

Judge William Sullivan sent jurors back to deliberate Tuesday after they first indicated they were struggling to agree. After the jury again reported that it was deadlocked, Sullivan delivered the formal charge.
A Tuey-Rodriguez charge is unique to Massachusetts and is sometimes called a "dynamite charge" because it is intended to help break a jury impasse without coercing a verdict.
LINDSAY CLANCY VERDICT STILL WITHIN REACH – RETIRED MASSACHUSETTS JUDGE PUSHES BACK ON HUNG-JURY PREDICTIONS
Lindsay Clancy arrives for day 3 of deliberations in her murder trial. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)

The instruction takes its name from two Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decisions. In Commonwealth v. Tuey (1851), the court approved an instruction encouraging deadlocked jurors to re-examine their views with an open mind. More than a century later, in Commonwealth v. Rodriguez (1973), the state's highest court revised that language to remove pressure on minority or holdout jurors, creating a neutral instruction that asks all jurors to carefully consider one another's views while maintaining their own honestly held convictions.

Receiving a Tuey-Rodriguez charge does not mean a verdict is imminent. The instruction is generally considered a necessary step before a judge declares a mistrial because of a hung jury, although it often results in jurors reaching a unanimous verdict after further deliberations.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S FUTURE COULD REST WITH ‘PROSECUTION DOCTORS’ AS CASE ECHOES INFAMOUS MAINE KILLINGS: EXPERT

Attorney Kevin Reddington holds up a display board of a text message Lindsay Clancy sent her mother, Paula, during her murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool via AP)
Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Thomas Drechsler told Fox News Digital the instruction is typically given only after a judge determines jurors have fully deliberated but remain deadlocked.

"The charge encourages the jurors to rethink their own feelings in light of what other jurors feel" while reminding them that no one is in a better position to decide the case than the jurors who heard all the evidence, Drechsler said.

If jurors report they remain deadlocked after receiving the instruction, "there's a higher likelihood" the case could end in a mistrial, Drechsler said, though he noted he has seen juries return verdicts after receiving a Tuey-Rodriguez charge.
Clancy faces three counts of first-degree murder in the January 2023 deaths of her three children — Cora, Dawson and Callan — at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home.

She does not dispute killing the children but argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible at the time. Prosecutors contend Clancy was legally sane and intentionally planned the killings.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague rested her case as defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked rebuttal witness Dr. Gregory Saathoff one last question during the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Jurors will continue deliberating after receiving the Tuey-Rodriguez charge. If they remain unable to reach a unanimous verdict, Sullivan could declare a mistrial, leaving prosecutors to decide whether to seek a new trial.

title: Where Tunnel to Towers' Steel Across America tour will stop ahead of 9/11
summary: A 21-foot steel beam from the South Tower of the World Trade Center heads to Fenway Park, D.C., and MetLife Stadium for the 9/11 anniversary.
story: Ground Zero steel from the World Trade Center's South Tower travels across America to educate younger generations about the tragedy of 9/11. Tunnel to Towers founder and CEO Frank Siller joins Jon Scott to discuss the emotional reactions of citizens touching the 17,000-pound beam during the foundation's memorial tour ahead of the September 11 anniversary.
A 21-foot steel beam recovered from the South Tower of the World Trade Center will make its way up the East Coast this week as part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation’s Steel Across America tour.

The tour kicked off earlier this year as a way to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and celebrate American service members and first responders. The steel will stop in Massachusetts, Washington, D.C., and New York City through Sept. 11.
Wednesday night's stop will be at the Boston Red Sox vs. Seattle Mariners game at Fenway Park in Boston, before heading to the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial on Thursday.

title: Tyler Robinson defense attorney should be ‘embarrassed’ for attacking Charlie Kirk as full of hate: lawyer
summary: Tyler Robinson's defense attorney called Charlie Kirk hateful in court, drawing sharp rebukes as the Kirk family watched during the preliminary hearing.
story: David Gelman weighs in after an attorney for the man accused of assassinating Charlie Kirk painted the victim as the hateful one during oral arguments Tuesday.

PROVO, Utah — A lawyer for the accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson drew rebukes inside and outside the courtroom Tuesday over remarks that painted the victim as the one behaving "hatefully" before he was shot and killed in front of thousands of people during a public speaking event at Utah Valley University.

"I think what the defense attorney said regarding Charlie Kirk and that he was full of hate, that was so unprofessional," said David Gelman, a New Jersey-based criminal defense attorney who has been following the case. "That was so out of left field that he honestly — he should be embarrassed of what he said."

Robinson, 23, is accused of assassinating the 31-year-old father of two at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, as Kirk was speaking in front of thousands of onlookers during a Turning Point USA event on campus.
TYLER ROBINSON HEARING COULD DECIDE DEATH PENALTY FATE, FINALLY SEE PLEA IN CHARLIE KIRK CASE

Defense attorney Richard Novak during closing arguments in the preliminary hearing as he turns towards Tyler Robinson, the man accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk, at the 4th District Court in Provo on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Francisco Kjolseth | The Salt Lake Tribune)

"Mr. Kirk spoke hatefully of certain groups of people," California-based defense attorney Richard Novak claimed during his argument against binding over the case for trial. He went on to say that there was a "significant gap" between what Kirk stood for and what Robinson felt about him.
WATCH: Tyler Robinson's attorney accuses Charlie Kirk of 'hate' while defending alleged assassin

As Novak repeated the phrase, Kirk's parents, widow and other relatives were in court. They exchanged looks and some teared up. Erika Kirk leaned forward and said something to an aide with the county attorney's office.
TYLER ROBINSON HEARING: TOP MOMENTS FROM EXPLOSIVE LANCE TWIGGS INTERVIEW PLAYED IN COURT

"You don't ever and I mean ever say that, No. 1, as a defense attorney or a prosecutor, especially not even at a trial," Gelman said. "If you want to paint Charlie as a bad person in front of the jury, knock your socks off. Do whatever you think you have to do. But to do that at a preliminary hearing...when you have the victim's family all there, that was totally uncalled for."

Attorney Jeffrey Neiman, representing the Kirk family, addresses the court in the Tyler Robinson case, who is charged in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, during closing arguments at his preliminary hearing in 4th District Court in Provo on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)
Chief Deputy Utah County Attorney Chad Grunander and Kirk family attorney Jeffrey Neiman both pushed back on Novak's comments in front of the judge.
CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

"The state takes great exception with Mr. Novak attributing all of this 'hate' to Mr. Kirk during his argument today," Grunander said in his rebuttal. "None of what was presented during the preliminary hearing [shows] that he is hateful towards this group or hateful towards that group. He had an opinion that he would express on politics and religion. That doesn't make it hate, but the fact that Mr. Novak even considered as hate makes the case for the state in his client's own words, he hated what Mr. Kirk stood for."
Neiman told the court that Kirk had made a career out of having "hard conversations" on difficult topics.
ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ALLEGEDLY CONFESSED IN TEXTS, APOLOGIZED AND DESCRIBED MOTIVE, AGENT TESTIFIES
Charlie Kirk and his wife, Erika Lane Frantzve, in an undated photo posted to social media. (Charlie Kirk via Instagram)
"Charlie was the opposite of hate," he said. "Firing a bullet into a crowd and assassinating him. That is hate."
In text messages prosecutors allege Robinson sent to Twiggs, the sender also accused Kirk of "hate."
Lance Twiggs, Robinson's roommate and romantic partner at the time, has been a key witness for prosecutors, who allege that Robinson confessed the crime and apparent motive to him.

"Why did I do it?" Robinson allegedly wrote to Twiggs after the slaying. "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out. If I am able to grab my rifle unseen, I will have left no evidence."

Charlie Kirk's parents, Kathryn Kirk, and Robert Kirk arrive at Utah's 4th District Court for preliminary hearing of Tyler Robinson in Provo, Utah, Tuesday, Sept 1, 2026. Robinson is charged with the murder of Charlie Kirk on the UVU campus last year.  (Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)
ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON ASKS JUDGE TO TAKE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY OFF TABLE
Fox News Digital has reached out to Robinson's defense team for comment.

"Charlie Kirk was not full of hatred," Gelman said. "If anything, he was full of love...He brought people together. He was there doing a free speech event, all right? He's trying to bring people on the left on the right together."

Judge Tony Graf Jr. bound over all charges to district court for trial Tuesday, including the death penalty-eligible charge of aggravated murder.

Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk spoke during his "American Comeback Tour" at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk was fatally shot while appearing at the event. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON FIGHTS BACK AS PROSECUTORS' SPRAWLING CASE COMES INTO FOCUS
Robinson is due back in court on Oct. 23 for a pretrial conference, where Graf may set a trial date.

His attorney, Kathy Nester, entered not guilty pleas on his behalf to all charges at an arraignment Tuesday.

title: Ohio Supreme Court denies Mackenzie Shirilla's latest appeal bid in double murder case
summary: Mackenzie Shirilla suffered another setback after the Ohio Supreme Court refused to reconsider its decision not to review her latest appeal.
story: Bryan Kohberger, accused in the quadruple murder of University of Idaho students, is attempting to withdraw his previous guilty plea. Kohberger's post-conviction petition alleges ineffective assistance of counsel, coercion, disinformation, and false promises, seeking a new trial. Victims' families, including Kaylee Goncalves' mother, expressed disappointment but noted they were not surprised by this latest legal maneuver.
Convicted double murderer Mackenzie Shirilla suffered another legal setback after the Ohio Supreme Court denied her attorneys' request to reconsider its decision not to hear her latest appeal.

Shirilla, now 21, is serving two concurrent sentences of 15 years to life for killing her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, 20, and their friend, Davion Flanagan, 19, after prosecutors said she intentionally drove her Toyota Camry into a brick building in Strongsville, Ohio, in 2022.

Chief Justice Sharon Kennedy denied Shirilla's motion for reconsideration after her attorneys asked the state's highest court to revisit its June 23 decision declining to review her case, according to court records.
"It is ordered by the court that the motion for reconsideration in this case is denied," Kennedy wrote.
MACKENZIE SHIRILLA'S TEXTS SURFACE AS 'HELL ON WHEELS' DRIVER'S APPEAL COLLIDES WITH NETFLIX'S 'THE CRASH'

Convicted killer Mackenzie Shirilla has landed a prison job while serving a life sentence for the 2022 crash that killed her boyfriend and their friend, Ohio prison officials confirmed to Fox News Digital. (Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction)
Tuesday's decision leaves intact a lower-court ruling that Shirilla's postconviction challenge was filed one day too late.
Shirilla's attorneys have argued that the missed deadline resulted from confusion over the filing timeline, including a calendar mistake involving the 2024 leap year.

The postconviction challenge sought to raise claims that Shirilla received ineffective assistance of counsel, including an argument that her trial lawyers failed to adequately investigate evidence that she suffered from Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome, or POTS.
Her attorneys have argued that the condition could have caused Shirilla to lose consciousness before the crash and potentially explain why she failed to brake before impact.
WATCH: MACKENZIE SHIRILLA’S FATHER CALLS HER ‘A DUMB 18-YEAR-OLD’ WHILE BERATING POLICE IN BODYCAM VIDEO
Mackenzie Shirilla makes a statement to the court during her sentencing in the Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court in Cleveland, Ohio on Monday, August 21, 2023. (Law&Crime livestream)
The defense previously said the condition was only "cursorily referenced" at trial despite Shirilla and her family allegedly putting her attorneys on notice about it.
The latest court decisions, however, have focused on whether Shirilla's postconviction petition was filed on time rather than the merits of those arguments.

Under Ohio law, a postconviction petition must generally be filed within 365 days after the trial transcript is filed in the court of appeals. The court determined that the relevant transcript was filed Oct. 24, 2023, making the deadline Oct. 23, 2024.
Shirilla filed her petition on Oct. 24, 2024, the 366th day.

Shirilla argued that the clock should have started later, when juvenile bindover transcripts were filed, and also pointed to the 2024 leap year. The appellate court rejected both arguments, finding that the statute refers to the "trial transcript," not supplemental juvenile-hearing transcripts, and that the law provides 365 days, not a calendar year.
IDAHO JUDGE GRANTS BRYAN KOHBERGER TWO HEARINGS NEXT YEAR AS ADMITTED KILLER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

Mackenzie Shirilla is serving two concurrent sentences of 15 years to life for the deaths of her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, and their friend, Davion Flanagan. (Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction)

Her attorneys later asked the Ohio Supreme Court to review the case. The state's highest court declined to accept jurisdiction June 23 before Shirilla's legal team asked the justices to reconsider that decision.
Shirilla's case has received renewed public attention following the release of Netflix's "The Crash."
Shirilla was convicted in 2023 after a bench trial of four counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and two counts of aggravated vehicular homicide.
Prosecutors argued at trial that Shirilla intentionally drove into the building to end her toxic relationship with Russo and that Flanagan was an unintended victim who happened to be in the car.
NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS ADAM MONTGOMERY'S MURDER CONVICTION IN DAUGHTER HARMONY'S DEATH

Mackenzie Shirlla was convicted of intentionally crashing her car into a brick wall to kill her boyfriend, Dominic Russo and his friend, Davion Flanagan. Shirilla posted the photo to Russo's online obituary. (Legacy.com)
Evidence presented in the case included surveillance video, vehicle "black box" data and evidence that Shirilla's car was traveling nearly 100 mph without braking before the crash, according to WOIO.
Shirilla has maintained that the crash was not intentional.
Her convictions were upheld on direct appeal in 2024.

A Haitian-born college student in Ohio died in what his family believes to be a suicide after he was stripped of his immigration status. (John Moore/Getty Images)

"He graduated from high school here," DeWine said. "He was well liked. He was in the junior ROTC. And, I’m told by those that knew him that he had great dreams about what he could do in this country and what he could contribute to this country."
"I think we have to ask ourselves: Is this really good? Is it what we want done to people like this being picked up and facing deportation? Do we want that being done in our name?" he asked.

Bel's father told The Haitian Times that his son was "distraught" after weeks of wearing an ankle monitor. He was among some Haitian immigrants in the Springfield, Ohio, area who have been required by the Department of Homeland Security to wear ankle monitors, after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the administration to end Haiti’s TPS designation, potentially exposing roughly 350,000 Haitian nationals to removal.

"In his last days, I did not recognize him as he was such an energetic kid who loves life, friends and family, and education," Bel's father, Pierre Ronal Bel, said in a statement read by Pastor Carl Ruby.
Bel's father said he was "treated like an animal" after receiving his ankle monitor, according to WSYX.
His father told The Washington Post that Bel left home before 8 a.m. on Monday and called shortly after to tell his father he was not feeling okay mentally.
"I told him, 'Come home so that we can talk?' I had my youngest to take to school. I took him to school," his father said.
But later that morning, police showed up at his home to inform him his son had died.
A month before his death, Bel spoke out about his experience wearing an ankle monitor.
HOUSE REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, SAYS ENDING HAITIAN TPS RISKS US HEALTHCARE 'CRISIS'

Pierre Damas Bel was among some Haitian immigrants in the Springfield, Ohio, area who have been required by the Department of Homeland Security to wear ankle monitors, after the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the administration to end Haiti’s TPS designation. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)
"I came to this country to pursue my education. I didn't come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone," he wrote on social media.

"Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience," he added. "I came here to study, to build my future and to live a better [life,] not to be treated like a criminal. So now, how am I supposed to play college sports with a GPS monitor on my leg?"
Ruby said on Monday that the family believes Bel took his own life as a result of President Donald Trump's immigration agenda that targeted TPS.
"I'm sitting with a family right now whose son threw himself in front of semi truck today after being teased by fellow students at Wright State about his ankle monitor," Ruby wrote on Facebook.

"I wish President Trump could hear the mom's wails. The family wants people to know that this was a suicide, and they want people to know that President Trump, [White House deputy chief of staff] Stephen Miller, and [Homeland Security Secretary] Markwayne Mullin’s inhumane immigration policies made this happen," the pastor continued.
Many of the roughly 15,000 Haitian immigrants in Springfield have lived in the U.S. for years, unable to return to their home country that has faced years of violence, turmoil and extreme poverty.
In a statement to WBTN, ICE said it "does not comment on the cause of death while that investigation is pending, and we will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals."

Springfield Pastor Carl Ruby said, "The family wants people to know that this was a suicide, and they want people to know that President Trump, [White House deputy chief of staff] Stephen Miller, and [Homeland Security Secretary] Markwayne Mullin’s inhumane immigration policies made this happen." (SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images)

Bel graduated from high school in May and was set to begin his first semester at Wright State University after being unable to play college soccer at Wittenberg University because of his ankle monitor, the Wittenberg men’s soccer team said in a Facebook post.

"He took 2 trips to Cincinnati and Westerville to plead to the officers to remove the bracelet since he’s a soccer player and he felt embarrassed and humiliated when he’s among his classmates at the University," Bel’s father wrote on X. "Last Friday, August 28, 2026, he told me, 'Dad I felt humiliated. Since they gave uniforms to all my classmates at JROTC their uniform, but except me because of the bracelet.'"
Wright State University President Sue Edwards said the school is "heartbroken by this devastating loss."

"Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community. The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time," Edwards said in a statement.

title: Lindsay Clancy verdict still within reach – retired Massachusetts judge pushes back on hung-jury predictions
summary: Lindsay Clancy murder trial jury reported a deadlock Tuesday, but a retired Massachusetts judge said a unanimous verdict remains very possible.
story: Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu pushed back on hung-jury predictions in the Lindsay Clancy trial, saying juries in emotional cases often report a deadlock before reaching a verdict. "There should be no rush to judgment," he said.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge pushed back on the notion that the Lindsay Clancy murder trial will end with a hung jury, saying a verdict is still possible despite Tuesday's deadlocked note from the jury.
Clancy, 36, faces three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan, all under age 6 — who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023.
Jurors went home Tuesday after more than 23 hours of deliberating over four days.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S FUTURE COULD REST WITH ‘PROSECUTION DOCTORS’ AS CASE ECHOES INFAMOUS MAINE KILLINGS: EXPERT
Lindsay Clancy watches the jury enter the room during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)
In a note sent to Judge William Sullivan on Tuesday, jurors said that "after many hours of deliberation, we are unable to come to a unanimous decision." He directed them to resume their work.

"I brought you back out because I know that this was a long trial. All right, I know there were over 80 witnesses. There were over 300 exhibits. Because of that, I'm going to ask you to go back out, keeping in mind all of the instructions that I gave you to go out and to continue your deliberations at this time. All right. And so, with that, I'm going to ask you to go back out. Like I said, keep in mind the instructions I gave you reviewing the evidence, and I'd ask you to resume your deliberations at this time," Sullivan said.
LINDSAY CLANCY VERDICT: RETIRED JUDGE EXPLAINS WHAT HAPPENS IF INSANITY DEFENSE PREVAILS

The jurors deliberating in Clancy's murder trial are discussing several options, which include first-degree murder, second-degree murder, voluntary or involuntary manslaughter, not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility (insanity) or not guilty.
Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital that the deadlock note doesn't necessarily signal a mistrial is likely, and said a verdict is still possible.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Lindsay Clancy sits at the defense table during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (David L. Ryan/Pool)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"It is common for juries that eventually reach a verdict, especially in highly emotional cases, to initially report that they are deadlocked. So you could see a unanimous verdict later in this case," Lu said. "There should be no rush to judgment."
SEND US A TIP

Superior Court Judge William Sullivan presides over day three of jury selection Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in the triple murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of murdering her three young children in 2023 in their Duxbury, Massachusetts home. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

"These jurors are deciding a difficult, difficult, difficult societal issue. No future jury and nobody else is going to be in a better position to decide these issues... it's a critical public service," he added.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Lu said that Sullivan was "150% correct" in not issuing a Tuey-Rodriguez charge to the jury today, which would have encouraged the jurors to keep deliberating toward a unanimous verdict. The instruction is used carefully in Massachusetts to avoid pressuring any individual juror, and Lu said giving it now would have been premature.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
The retired judge said it was "still a little early" to read the deadlock as a sign the jury will ultimately hang.
LINDSAY CLANCY DIDN'T SHOW 'BREAK WITH REALITY' AS JURY WEIGHS PSYCHOSIS DEFENSE: SUSAN SMITH PROSECUTOR
"It's still too early, and we could go much longer on these deliberations, and it would be totally legitimate," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Jurors will return on Wednesday morning at 9 a.m. to resume deliberations.
Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

title: Washington homeowner hears mysterious banging, calls 911 before police find growling bobcat at top of stairs
summary: Video shows a growling bobcat perched atop a Washington homeowner's staircase after police responded to a reported burglary in a neighborhood.
story: Kirkland police deployed a drone to track a bobcat inside a resident’s home before officers safely contained the unexpected intruder and wildlife officials later released it. (Credit: Kirkland Police Department)

A Washington homeowner who heard mysterious banging inside their house called 911 to report a possible burglary, only for responding officers to discover the "cat burglar" was quite literal — a bobcat perched at the top of the stairs.

The unusual encounter unfolded last week in Kirkland's Moss Bay neighborhood, where police were ultimately able to corral the wild animal before wildlife officials later returned it to its natural habitat.
No injuries were reported to the homeowner, responding officers or the bobcat, according to the Kirkland Police Department.
COLORADO FAMILY WAKES UP TO BEAR EATING BREAKFAST IN KITCHEN
Officers deployed a drone to monitor a bobcat's movements inside a Kirkland home while keeping a safe distance from the wild animal. (Kirkland Police Department)
Police said they responded to a report of a possible burglary after the resident reported hearing banging inside the home. When officers arrived, they discovered the bobcat inside.
Authorities deployed a drone to monitor the bobcat's movements inside the home, allowing officers to maintain a safe distance and coordinate their response.
BLACK BEAR CAUGHT ON VIDEO WANDERING INTO CALIFORNIA WATER DISTRICT OFFICE AFTER PUSHING OPEN FRONT DOOR
Officers safely corralled the bobcat into an isolated room until wildlife officials arrived to sedate the animal. (Kirkland Police Department)
Video released by Kirkland police shows the bobcat growling while perched at the top of the staircase.
The unexpected house guest was safely corralled into an isolated room until the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife arrived.
After being sedated, the bobcat was later released near Forbes Creek, close to the natural habitat where it was found, police said.
Police believe the bobcat climbed a tree and jumped through an open window, possibly after being drawn inside by the homeowner's cat.
CALIFORNIA COUPLE FIGHTS OFF 70-POUND BLACK BEAR WITH HATCHET AND WATER BOTTLE OUTSIDE THEIR HOME
Wildlife officials released the bobcat near Forbes Creek after it was safely removed from a home in Kirkland, Washington. (Kirkland Police Department)
The resident's cat was later found unharmed.
Officials warned residents never to approach or feed a bobcat and to give the animal plenty of space if encountered.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife also recommends that residents keep pets indoors, especially between dusk and dawn, and secure small livestock and poultry.

title: Tyler Robinson to face trial in Charlie Kirk assassination as judge keeps death penalty on table
summary: A Utah judge ruled prosecutors presented enough evidence for trial on all seven counts against Tyler Robinson in Charlie Kirk's fatal shooting.
story: Fox News correspondent Garrett Tenney has the latest on a Utah judge's ruling that accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson will stand trial on aggravated murder charges and remain eligible for the death penalty, after prosecutors argued he knowingly endangered others during the 2025 shooting at a Turning Point USA event, on 'Jesse Watters Primetime.'

Tyler Robinson, the man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will stand trial after a Utah judge ruled Tuesday that prosecutors presented enough evidence to move forward on all seven charges against him.

Robinson pleaded not guilty to all charges moments after Judge Tony Graf issued the ruling. Graf also ruled that prosecutors may continue seeking the death penalty in the case. He found that the state established probable cause for the victim-targeting allegation, allowing the capital sentencing enhancement to move forward.

"Viewed in the light most favorable to the prosecution, this evidence is sufficient at this stage to support a reasonable belief that the defendant is the individual who shot and killed Charlie Kirk," Graf said.
TYLER ROBINSON HEARING COULD DECIDE DEATH PENALTY FATE, FINALLY SEE PLEA IN CHARLIE KIRK CASE

Robinson, charged in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, speaks with defense attorney Staci Visser, as Deputy Utah County Attorney Chad Grunander offers a rebuttal during closing arguments in 4th District Court in Provo on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)

Graf emphasized that the standard at a preliminary hearing is not whether prosecutors have proven their case beyond a reasonable doubt, but whether there is enough evidence to send the charges to trial.
"Whether the state can prove the aggravating circumstance beyond a reasonable doubt remains for trial," Graf said. "Count one is bound over for trial."
PROSECUTORS HAMMER TYLER ROBINSON'S BID TO DERAIL DEATH PENALTY IN CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE
Tyler Robinson pleaded not guilty to all seven charges filed by prosecutors. (Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)
The judge also sided with prosecutors on the victim-targeting allegation against Robinson, concluding that the state had established probable cause for the allegation.

Graf ultimately ordered Robinson to stand trial on all seven charges: aggravated murder; felony discharge of a firearm causing serious bodily injury; two counts of obstruction of justice; two counts of witness tampering; and committing a violent offense in the presence of a child.
CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

Tyler Robinson, charged in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, sits during closing arguments at his preliminary hearing in 4th District Court in Provo on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)

The aggravated murder and firearm charges are first-degree felonies, while the obstruction charges are second-degree felonies and the witness tampering charges are third-degree felonies. The final charge,committing a violent offense in the presence of a child, is a Class A misdemeanor.
The court moved directly into Robinson’s arraignment after Graf issued his ruling. The defense waived a formal reading of the charges, and Robinson’s attorney entered not guilty pleas on his behalf.
The ruling came hours after another courtroom fight over whether cameras should be allowed to remain in the high-profile proceedings.
Following closed-door arguments Tuesday morning and additional arguments in open court, Graf again denied a defense motion seeking to remove cameras from the courtroom.
Robinson’s attorneys had raised concerns about the intense publicity surrounding the case, including what they described as online marketplace gambling tied to its outcome.
ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON DEALT COURTROOM BLOW, DAYS BEFORE PIVOTAL HEARING
Graf ruled cameras could remain, subject to the restrictions laid out in his courtroom decorum order.

Kirk, 31, was shot and killed Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking before thousands at an outdoor Turning Point USA event at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. Prosecutors have accused Robinson of firing the fatal shot from an elevated position overlooking the crowd.
ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON FIGHTS BACK AS PROSECUTORS' SPRAWLING CASE COMES INTO FOCUS

Erika Kirk departs court in Provo, Utah, Monday, July 6, 2026. The widow of Charlie Kirk was attending the first day of preliminary hearings against, Tyler Robinson who is on trial for Kirk's murder. (Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)

Before Tuesday’s hearing ended, Jeff Neiman, an attorney representing Kirk’s family, urged the court to move the case toward trial without unnecessary delays and pushed back against comments defense attorney Richard Novak made about Kirk.
"Charlie devoted his life to building a community of over a million young people rooted in faith and freedom. He had hard conversations others were too afraid to have," Neiman told the court.
ERIKA KIRK COMFORTS A STRANGER IN TEARS DURING HEARING FOR HUSBAND'S ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON

Charlie Kirk throws hats to the crowd after arriving at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, on Sept. 10, 2025. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
"Charlie was the opposite of hate," he continued. "Firing a bullet into a crowd and assassinating him. That is hate."
Neiman said Kirk’s family recognizes Robinson’s right to a fair trial but wants the case to move forward swiftly.
UTAH PROSECUTORS ASK JUDGE TO SHUT DOWN DELAY TACTICS IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION CASE

"The United States Constitution guarantees criminal defendants many rights. The right to delay is not among them," Neiman said. "The defendant is entitled to a fair trial, and he must be given one. But nothing more is owed."
"We have no doubt this court will give the defendant a fair trial," he added. "We ask that it do so swiftly."
Neiman later specifically asked Graf to set a trial date at Robinson’s next court appearance so Kirk’s family would know when the case is expected to move forward.
Jeffrey Neiman arrives to court in Provo, Utah, Tuesday, Sept 1, 2026. (Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Robinson is due back in court Oct. 23 at 1 p.m. local time for a status conference and has been ordered to appear. A trial date could be set at that hearing.
Following Tuesday's hearing, Kirk's family said Graf's decision to send Robinson to trial marks "an important step" in their pursuit of justice nearly one year after Kirk's death.
"Today's decision, which comes nearly a year since Charlie was taken from us, marks an important step in our family's pursuit of justice for him," the family said in a statement.
The family said every stage of the case has carried "the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken," especially for Kirk's children, who "will grow up without their father."
As the case moves toward trial, the family said they remain committed to seeking justice for Charlie while praying for "a transparent and timely process."
Fox News' Lee Ross contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Ohio man accused of vandalizing JD Vance’s home pleads guilty
summary: The Ohio man was detained by Secret Service agents after allegedly using a hammer to attack JD Vance’s residence and a federal vehicle.
story: A North Dakota man has been charged with felony criminal mischief after police say he keyed a Tesla Cybertruck in West Fargo. (Mitch Benson via Storyful)
An Ohio man accused of vandalizing Vice President JD Vance’s Cincinnati home earlier this year pleaded guilty in federal court Tuesday, officials said.
William D. DeFoor, 26, reportedly caused tens of thousands of dollars in damage Jan. 5 when he used a hammer to smash multiple windows at Vance’s unoccupied home.

DeFoor specifically admitted to acts of physical violence against government officials or property, as well as the willful injury or depredation of U.S. government property, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Ohio.

His defense attorney previously said the assaults were not politically motivated and that DeFoor suffers from mental health issues. Court records show DeFoor has a history of criminal cases involving findings of mental incompetency.
SUSPECT IN VANCE HOME VANDALISM HAS HAD MULTIPLE RUN-INS WITH THE LAW, DEMANDED TO BE CALLED JULIA
William D. DeFoor remained jailed for nearly nine months after allegedly vandalizing Vice President JD Vance’s Cincinnati home. (WXIX; Hamilton County Sheriff's Office)

"Perpetrators like DeFoor, who put that freedom at risk, particularly through violent, destructive actions, will, like here, be vigorously prosecuted," U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II said in a statement Tuesday.

According to court documents, DeFoor was detained around midnight after Secret Service agents observed him near the front fence of Vance’s protected residence. Vance and his family were in Washington, D.C., at the time of the incident.
SECRET SERVICE AGENT ON JD VANCE'S DETAIL INVESTIGATED FOR ALLEGEDLY LEAKING OPERATIONAL SECURITY INFO

While wielding a hammer, DeFoor reportedly breached the property line at the driveway and proceeded to target an unmarked federal law enforcement vehicle blocking the driveway entrance. DeFoor used the weapon to strike the driver’s side window three times, prosecutors said.
As Secret Service agents responded, DeFoor ignored all commands to stop and drop the weapon, according to charging documents.
He then used the hammer to break large, historic glass windows across the front of the home, officials said.
The attack reportedly damaged components of an enhanced security system located on each window. The equipment was owned by the U.S. government and valued at more than $28,000, prosecutors said.
ATTORNEY FOR SUSPECT IN VANCE HOME VANDALISM RULES OUT POSSIBLE MOTIVATION
William DeFoor, 26, appears in court Jan. 6, 2026, for non-federal charges in the vandalism of Vice President JD Vance's Cincinnati home. (WXIX)
Secret Service agents and Cincinnati police officers eventually detained DeFoor after he tried to flee on foot.
Gerace on Tuesday further condemned the violence, saying assaults against U.S. officials will be prosecuted.

"Acts of violence directed against our political leaders, their families or property, have no place in our society and will not be tolerated. Our elected leaders, at all levels of government, must be permitted to carry out their duties free from threats, vandalism and other forms of violence," Gerace said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
According to court records, DeFoor has a history of mental health issues in Hamilton County spanning more than two years.
FBI sources previously told Fox News that when DeFoor was arrested, he demanded to be called "Julia."

In April 2023, DeFoor was charged with trespassing at University of Cincinnati Health Psychiatric Emergency Services after police said he refused to leave the premises. He was ruled incompetent to stand trial, and the case was later dismissed.

The following year, DeFoor was charged with two counts of vandalism after windows at a Hyde Park business were broken. The case was referred to a mental health docket, with treatment ordered in lieu of conviction.
Vice President JD Vance and his family were in Washington, D.C., when his Cincinnati home was vandalized. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Hamilton County Court later approved an application granting DeFoor’s mother legal guardianship after finding him incompetent by reason of mental illness.
Fox News Digital’s Stephen Sorace and Greg Wehner contributed to this report.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Ohio woman learns fate in fatal dragging of driver who climbed onto her hood in road rage death
summary: Danielle Henry was driving a stolen car after shoplifting at a Kroger in Westerville when a parking lot fender bender turned into a fatal encounter.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
An Ohio woman who dragged a DoorDash driver to his death following a fender bender in a grocery store parking lot was sentenced last week to up to 5½ years in prison.
Danielle Henry was handed the sentence after pleading guilty last month to aggravated vehicular homicide in the death of 38-year-old Ibrahim Diakite, WBNS-TV reported.
Henry had just shoplifted and was driving a stolen car when she collided with Diakite in October 2025 at a Kroger parking lot in Westerville.
The incident escalated, authorities said, when Henry fled in her vehicle.
PREGNANT WOMAN DRIVING HOME FROM PRENATAL VISIT SHOT DURING ALLEGED ROAD RAGE ATTACK: POLICE

Danielle Henry was sentenced to 5½ years in prison for the road rage death of a Door Dash driver who was dragged and run over during an October 2025 confrontation in Ohio. (Franklin County Sheriff's Office)
Diakite followed and pulled up in front of her at a stoplight. He got out and stopped in front of Henry's vehicle in an effort to prevent her from leaving. He then climbed onto the hood of the car.
Henry drove off and sped up to 45 mph before jerking the car. Diakite was pulled under the vehicle and dragged for about 300 to 600 feet before he was run over, authorities said.
TEXAS DOORDASH DRIVER GETS HIT BY A CAR FLEEING FROM POLICE AND STILL DELIVERS THE ORDER
Diakite was later pronounced dead at a hospital.
At the time of the road rage incident, Henry had several active warrants, for charges of theft, receiving stolen property and failure to comply with police.
Danielle Henry was sentenced to 5½ years in prison. (iStock)

"She was obviously willing to do whatever she could to keep from being caught by the police and showed herself to be a danger to the community," Westerville Police Chief Holly Murchland told the news outlet.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Henry will be required to serve at least four years, and her driver's license was permanently suspended.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Ex-Indiana deputy charged with felony for allegedly using Flock cameras to stalk girlfriend
summary: Skylar Thompson allegedly ran over 2,000 Flock camera searches on his girlfriend's license plate, falsely listing them as city planning duties.
story: Fox News correspondent Danamarie McNicholl has the latest on police officers across the country being arrested for allegedly misusing Flock Safety camera systems as growing concerns over privacy and accountability fuel scrutiny of the license plate reader technology and its use by law enforcement agencies nationwide on 'America Reports.'

A former Indiana sheriff's deputy was charged with abusing access to Flock camera technology to stalk his girlfriend for over the period of a year by allegedly conducting more than 2,000 searches for her license plate.
Skylar Thompson, 31, faces one count of official misconduct as a Level 6 felony and a misdemeanor count of fraud.

The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department discovered that Thompson used the Flock technology to conduct the searches between Dec. 31, 2025, and Aug. 2 during an internal audit of the system, the Jackson County Prosecutor's Office said.
POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN'

Skylar Thompson, 31, a former Indiana sheriff's deputy, was charged with allegedly conducting more than 2,000 searches for the same license plate using Flock cameras, prosecutors said. (Getty Images; Jackson County Prosecutor's Office)
Thompson reportedly listed his searches as "city planning/traffic analysis" despite never being assigned tasks involving either duty, prosecutors said.
The agency then asked the Indiana State Police to investigate. Thompson turned himself in to authorities Monday.
He resigned from the sheriff's department the day he was confronted about the alleged abuse. He also drove to his girlfriend's home and admitted what he had done, WKBN-TV reported.
FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES
Flock cameras are used in towns across the nation as license plate readers, but the technology has come under scrutiny in recent months. (Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty Images, File)

"Law enforcement officers are entrusted with access to sensitive information and investigative tools, and that access must be used responsibly and only for legitimate law enforcement purposes," the Jackson County Prosecutor’s Office said. "No person is above the law, including those entrusted with enforcing it."
Flock cameras have come under heavy scrutiny over privacy concerns and the potential for misuse.
Flock Safety spokesperson Paris Lewbel defended the technology as an important public safety tool in a statement to Fox News Digital last month.

"Flock’s technology is an important public safety tool for law enforcement agencies across Texas, helping officers solve serious crimes, find missing people, recover stolen vehicles and support safer communities," Lewbel said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We support thoughtful legislation and strong privacy, transparency and accountability guardrails that ensure technology is used responsibly while preserving law enforcement’s ability to use effective tools to keep people safe."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Swimmer rushed to hospital after suspected shark attack at Martha’s Vineyard
summary: Swimming was temporarily suspended at South Beach in Edgartown after a woman sustained injuries considered consistent with a potential shark bite.
story: Faith Tenkley, 23, safely landed in the Atlantic Ocean near Boca Raton after a right-engine failure and broken landing gear. (Credit: SCHD STAN | Craig Sutton/@SCHDETF)
Emergency personnel from Martha’s Vineyard rushed a swimmer to a hospital Monday after the woman sustained what appeared to be a shark bite, officials said.
The incident happened in the afternoon at South Beach in Edgartown, Massachusetts, along one of the island’s most popular shorelines.
Officials said the victim, in her late 20s, was in the water when she suffered a wound to her lower leg.
SHARK WEEK PUTS SHARK BITE SURVIVAL IN FOCUS WITH ER DOC'S EXPERT TIPS

A sign warned beachgoers that a shark had been spotted along South Beach in Martha’s Vineyard July 11, 2008. A woman was wounded Monday in a suspected shark encounter at the beach. (Stuart Cahill/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images)
"Based upon the nature of the injuries, however, the wounds were considered consistent with a potential shark bite," Town Administrator James Hagerty said in a statement.
Her injuries were considered non-life-threatening and "did not involve the loss of a limb or other life-threatening trauma," Hagerty said.
Multiple Edgartown agencies responded, and the woman received initial medical treatment before being transported to a hospital for further care.
After the suspected shark encounter, no marine predators were observed or confirmed that were involved the incident, officials said.
SHARK SIGHTINGS SPIKE NEAR AMERICA'S BEACHES AS JULY 4 CROWDS HEAD TO SHORE FOR WEEKEND
In accordance with town protocol, officials suspended swimming at South Beach for several hours as a precaution, allowing personnel to assess conditions before later lifting the water restrictions.
The town thanked emergency personnel and beach staff for their prompt response.
SHARK WEEK WARNINGS AS EXPERTS REVEAL 6 WAYS TO REDUCE YOUR RISK OF A SHARK BITE

A man watches the sunset from a lifeguard tower at South Beach State Park in Edgartown, Mass., Aug. 17, 2015. Swimming at South Beach was temporarily restricted Aug. 31, 2026, after a suspected shark attack. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
"Beachgoers are reminded to remain aware of their surroundings while in the water and to comply with instructions from lifeguards and any posted beach advisories," Hagerty said.
Confirmed shark attacks near Martha’s Vineyard have historically been rare, though marine predators are known to pass through the area.
Nearly all serious or fatal shark attacks in Massachusetts over the last two decades have occurred along the coast of nearby Cape Cod, which is two hours away by car.

Seals poke their heads out of the water near Skiff Island, just offshore from South Beach near Martha’s Vineyard. Seals along the Massachusetts coastline can attract great white sharks to the area. (Stuart Cahill/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images/File)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Cape Cod is considered a major hot spot for great white sharks in the North Atlantic due to its large population of gray seals, a primary food source for the predators.

title: Coast Guard rescues 37 suspected migrants stranded for 2 days off California coast
summary: A 30-foot pleasure craft with 37 suspected migrants drifted for two days without fuel, food or water nearly 90 miles off Southern California.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

FIRST ON FOX: Dozens of suspected migrants were rescued from a 30-foot pleasure craft after spending two days stranded without fuel, food or water, nearly 90 miles off the Southern California coast, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
The Coast Guard said 37 suspected migrants were aboard the boat when crews reached it Friday, about 88 miles from Channel Islands Harbor.
The rescue began around 3:40 p.m., when the boat’s operator radioed the Coast Guard for help.
OVERCROWDED MIGRANT VESSEL WITH 240 PEOPLE ON BOARD INTERCEPTED NEAR TURKS AND CAICOS
The Coast Guard brought the suspected migrant group ashore and turned them over to U.S. Border Patrol personnel. (U.S. Coast Guard)
The operator said the boat had been drifting for two days without fuel, food or water and had no personal safety equipment.
The suspected migrants were adrift without fuel, food or water for two days, the Coast Guard said. (U.S. Coast Guard)
The Coast Guard sent several crews to the area, including the cutters Sockeye and Halibut, boats from stations in Los Angeles-Long Beach and Channel Islands, and an air crew.
Crews found the boat around 8:30 p.m. and brought all 37 suspected migrants aboard the Sockeye.
The 37 suspected migrants were rescued from a 30-foot pleasure craft about 90 miles off Southern California's coast, the Coast Guard said. (U.S. Coast Guard)
"I could not be prouder of the Coast Guard crews on scene who were directly responsible for 37 lives saved last night," said Master Chief Peter Nelson, the Sockeye’s officer in charge.
COAST GUARD SEIZES 7K POUNDS OF COCAINE WORTH MORE THAN $54 MILLION NEAR PUERTO RICO, FIVE ARRESTED
The Coast Guard brought all 37 suspected migrants to Coast Guard Base Los Angeles-Long Beach, where they were turned over to U.S. Border Patrol. (U.S. Coast Guard)
Nelson said crews carried out the rescue at night in rough conditions far from shore.

"Despite operating far offshore in rough conditions at night, they persevered until every person in danger was rescued," Nelson said. "Their extraordinary professionalism, superb judgment, and impeccable seamanship shined throughout the entire case."
The Sockeye brought the group to Coast Guard Base Los Angeles-Long Beach, where they were turned over to U.S. Border Patrol.
The Coast Guard did not say where the group was from, where the boat began its journey or where it was headed. (U.S. Coast Guard)

The Coast Guard did not immediately say where the group was from, where the boat began its journey or where it was headed.

title: North Carolina climber airlifted after plunging 20 feet down gorge, sustaining serious injuries
summary: A climber fell 20 feet on Shortoff Mountain in North Carolina's Linville Gorge, triggering a massive Black Hawk helicopter airlift to Charlotte.
story: The climber sustained serious injuries while climbing near Shortoff Mountain in Linville Gorge. (Credit: Facebook @ Burke Rescue Inc and SAR)
A hiker who fell 20 feet in a North Carolina gorge and sustained serious injuries was airlifted out of harm’s way over the weekend.
Emergency crews were called around 2 p.m. Sunday amid reports of a fallen climber along a steep section of Shortoff Mountain in Linville Gorge.

"The lead climber was attempting to place gear approximately 40 feet above the ledge when they took a lead fall of approximately 15–20 feet," Burke Rescue Inc. and SAR posted on its Facebook page, "during which they swung away from the climbing wall and struck an adjacent rock pillar."
An online fundraiser shared by Burke Rescue identified the climber as Jacob Gregory.
HELICOPTER RESCUE CREW CAUGHT ON CAMERA SAVING 2 CLIMBERS TRAPPED ALONG POPULAR CALIFORNIA BEACH CLIFF
Emergency crews airlifted a climber who fell over the weekend while climbing Linville Gorge in North Carolina. (Burke Rescue Inc and SAR)
Paramedics initially responded, rappelled down to the climber, and assessed the patient while additional resources were requested.

"After a request for whole blood, a Burke Rescue volunteer ran approximately 1.5 miles, covering 1,000 feet of elevation in just 31 minutes," the Facebook post states, "while carrying critical whole blood to the patient to help stabilize them for transport."
AMERICAN RED CROSS DECLARES NATIONAL BLOOD CRISIS AS TYPE O SUPPLY DROPS TO DANGEROUS LEVELS
Emergency crews seen during an airlift rescue in North Carolina of a climber who fell while hiking. (Burke Rescue Inc and SAR)
A North Carolina Helo-Aquatic Rescue Team Black Hawk helicopter was eventually called to assist with an air rescue because of the steep, rugged terrain.
The helicopter, known as "Kill Devil 244," lifted the climber off the mountain and took him to Charlotte for medical treatment. The rescue involved two dozen agencies from surrounding counties.
RESCUERS FREE CLIMBER TRAPPED BENEATH 16,000-POUND BOULDER ON OREGON'S MOUNT HOOD IN COMPLEX OPERATION

"It took an extraordinary number of people, coordination, and courage to get Jacob from that remote mountainside to the care he needed," the online fundraiser said. "To every responder who answered that call: thank you. You saved a life and brought a husband, father, brother, son, friend and loved one to safety."
A climber was airlifted to safety on Sunday and falling 20 feet while on a mountain. (Burke Rescue Inc and SAR)

Burke Rescue noted that climbing comes with inherent risks and urged climbers to "know your abilities" as well as use appropriate equipment.

title: Suspect in custody for strangling Massachusetts woman to death in her home is Brazilian illegal immigrant
summary: Flavio Alcantara Dias called 911 saying he killed Brianna Connolly in her Framingham home, officials say. ICE says he was released under the Biden administration.
story: Salvadoran national Alexis Antonio Cedillos-Campos faces a premeditated murder charge in the fatal stabbing of Virginia mother Carmen Lizet Puch. Fairfax County police say the 19-year-old suspect confessed to the killing and had previously been released at the border. Authorities say Cedillos-Campos and Puch worked together and had been in an intimate relationship before the fatal attack.
Federal authorities say they arrested an illegal immigrant accused of strangling a woman to death inside her Massachusetts home on Tuesday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement say Flavio Alcantara Dias, 43, is an illegal immigrant from Brazil who was released into the U.S. under former President Joe Biden's administration, despite previous arrests for DUI and aggravated assault.

"Alcantara Dias illegally entered the United States in April 2019. In October 2024, an immigration judge granted Alcantara Dias’ motion to terminate his immigration hearings based on a technicality, bringing his immigration case to an end despite his criminal history and unlawful presence in the United States. He was then released into the country by the Biden administration," the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement.
BIDEN ADMIN RELEASED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED OF FATALLY STABBING FAIRFAX COUNTY MOTHER

Federal law enforcement officers with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) conduct a traffic stop and detain people, Nov. 17, 2025, in Washington. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

We are urging the Framingham Police Department to participate in a controlled transfer of this criminal illegal alien to get him out of our communities once and for all," the statement continued.
"Our message is clear: if you come into our country illegally and break our laws, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you," DHS added.
EXCLUSIVE: LEGAL GROUP TELLS NYPD COPS THEY CAN CONTACT ICE DIRECTLY DESPITE BLUE CITY'S SANCTUARY RULES

ICE LODGES DETAINER FOR ILLEGAL MIGRANT CHARGED WITH STRANGLING WIFE AND DUMPING BODY NEAR OKLAHOMA HIGHWAY
"He then states, ‘I ended up killing a woman by mistake.’ He says, ‘I went crazy and suffocated her later on, says that he strangled her,’" Brandt said, noting that Dias had been speaking Portuguese.

The Homeland Security logo appears on the screen of a smartphone, and in the background, the flag of the United States is on the computer screen on Dec. 3, 2024. (Jaque Silva/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

story: Student says task force reforms

The suspect was taken into custody by the Massachusetts State Police, Cambridge Police Department director of communications Jennie Lopez told The Harvard Crimson. No injuries were reported.

Lopez told Fox News Digital that the man brandished the weapon at a coffee shop in Harvard Square shortly after 8:45 a.m. She clarified that the weapon was not a machete, contrary to earlier local media reports.
