title: Arizona congressman heard ‘freight train crash’ sound during Grand Canyon flash flood
summary: Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.
story: Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.
Schweikert told NBC News from his office in Washington on Tuesday that the loud crash was followed by a powerful stream of mud and debris-filled water.

Two visitors died and another is still missing after flash flooding from a sudden deluge of rain briefly transformed Bright Angel Creek into a full-fledged river. About 80 people were evacuated from campsites around the historic Phantom Ranch area of the park.

The retiring member of Congress and the rest of his group were about 100 yards away from the danger zone without cellphone service. His guide led the group to an area off the Colorado River near Bright Angel Creek.
They later left the area on foot — traveling on higher ground — and camped for the night nearby.

It is “monsoon season” in Arizona, but Schweikert said there was not more than a drizzle of precipitation where he was when the dangerous flood ripped through, underscoring the potential randomness of such events.
“At some point, you realized this is a big deal; something’s really gone haywire. ... It was a ginormous flash flood,” he said.
The intricate terrain of the Grand Canyon can invite the type of deadly flood conditions that hit the southern part of the national park over the weekend.
“The deluge downpour could have been miles away and was channeled into the canyon, and what used to be a creek now is a river,” said Schweikert, who is a regular Grand Canyon hiker.
The water supply system for the park was also severely damaged, along with part of a new $208 million water pipeline project that was underway near the ranch.
Schweikert said he would likely be involved in working to get the damage addressed once proper assessments are made. “Right now, the heartbreak is a couple of people lost their lives,” he added.

He also cautioned visitors to the park to carefully monitor the weather and to use extreme caution if storms are expected in the vicinity at all. If storms are nearby, hikes through narrow passages known as slot canyons should be strictly avoided because of the risk of getting trapped, the seasoned adventurer said.
“It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Schweikert said.

title: Thousands of U.S. service members arrive in Thailand after record stint at sea
summary: About 5,000 U.S. sailors and Marines are stopping in the resort city of Pattaya for a “rest and relaxation” break as they return home from a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.
story: LAEM CHABANG, Thailand — The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived Wednesday at a port in eastern Thailand, where thousands of U.S. sailors and Marines are disembarking for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.

The toll of the more than nine-month deployment, most of it spent supporting military operations in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, was visible on the carrier as it pulled into Laem Chabang Port in Chonburi province. Paint has worn off and the metal underneath is rusted on the 1,092-foot warship, which is one of the largest in the world.

The Lincoln is in Thailand for a four-day “rest and relaxation” stop on its way home to San Diego after having spent weeks in the headlines as the lengthy deployment raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health.

The U.S. Navy confirmed the ship’s arrival in a statement, saying the Lincoln strike group arrived in Laem Chabang while the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. docked in nearby Sriracha and the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls went to Map Ta Phut in neighboring Rayong province.
The Navy said it was the Lincoln’s first full port stop after 286 days at sea since the deployment began in November.

“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” said Rear Adm. Robert E. Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3. “It also underscores the strong and enduring partnership and alliance between the United States and Thailand.”

About 5,000 sailors and Marines are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya, a nearby coastal resort city that is one of the most popular tourist destinations in Thailand. Each service member will get three “liberty days” and one day of duty aboard the ship, a U.S. military official said.

Upon the Lincoln’s arrival in the morning, service members could be seen working aboard the deck as loudspeakers played announcements about the process for disembarkation. A whistle could be heard ringing across the deck, a Navy tradition that signals coming ashore.
Thai police crackdown on sex workers

Around 1 p.m. local time (2 a.m. ET), service members began disembarking from the ship in civilian clothes, some carrying backpacks. One service member was carrying his golf clubs. Waiting for them across the way were dozens of Ford pickup trucks and buses lined up in columns to take them into town.
“Please be on your best behavior,” a commanding officer could be heard saying over loudspeaker.

Locals in tourism-dependent Pattaya have eagerly awaited the arrival of the Lincoln, which pulled into sight from the shore after sunrise before it made a wide turn and harbored itself at a major cargo terminal.

Officials in Pattaya, where international tourist arrivals have dropped because of travel disruptions and soaring fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, say the visit is expected to inject about $3 million into the local economy.

Authorities in Pattaya have stepped up security, with heightened police patrols and checks along the roads. Businesses here are also trying to woo the sailors, with some putting up banners to welcome them.
Wichai Yuankham, 35, a factory worker who came to watch the ships arrive, said the naval visit was a welcome boost to the local economy.
“I am just excited to see the destroyer docking,” he said. “This is my first time seeing the destroyer, and I feel good seeing it, and we can boast to our neighboring countries about this.”

title: Customers are losing their appetites over disturbing AI-generated menus
summary: AI “slop” is increasingly on offer at brick-and-mortar establishments.
story: AI “slop” is now increasingly on offer at brick-and-mortar establishments.

As AI image-making technology has grown more advanced — and cheaper to use, in some cases being free — images with a distinct “slop” flavor, namely ones with surreal or even disturbing attributes, have begun appearing on bodega, café and restaurant menus.
There’s the shrimp scampi whose shrimp look more like miniature life preservers.
A breakfast burrito with filling that looks more like something out of a horror movie.
And “protein” options that look like they’re covered in bugs.
One X user said she attempted to order an item advertised on a café’s outdoor menu only to learn it didn’t exist and was instead the product of ChatGPT.

The trend comes as the use of AI has grown from a tech-employee specialty to a nearly ubiquitous pursuit among white-collar workers — and as overall inflation in the economy has remained stubborn. The confluence of lingering cost pressures and advancing technology appears to be translating into a boom in smaller businesses deploying AI-designed graphics and logos.

There have been real-world consequences to the trend of AI slop making the jump from online into the real world. A coffee shop in San Francisco paid hundreds of dollars to have graffiti removed that appeared to be in response to its use of AI-generated food images on its facade, SFGate reported.

“I want people to come to our restaurant, but, like, why is this such a big deal that it influences people on such intense level?” co-owner Lyndsey Lozano told the outlet. “Like, is it really that horrific that you have to act on such a feeling?”
Lozano could not be reached for additional comment.

Many of the establishments displaying the food images likely created by AI are smaller, likely family-owned establishments, said Paul Shovlin, an assistant professor of English at Ohio University who studies AI. He said that it may simply be the case that many of the places displaying the AI food are running on shoestring budgets.
For some longtime designers, the advent of AI-related image making has been maddening — not to mention bad for their bottom lines.

title: JD Vance talks end times, Antichrist and AI on faith podcast
summary: Vice President JD Vance warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence Tuesday and said he wouldn’t be “shocked” if we were living in the “end times” and the Antichrist was walking the Earth.
story: Vice President JD Vance warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence Tuesday and said he wouldn’t be “shocked” if we were living in the “end times” and the Antichrist was walking the Earth.
Vance made the remarks in a wide-ranging interview on faith with popular Christian podcaster Bryce Crawford.
During the hour long sitdown, Crawford asked Vance his perspective on whether the end times are coming — or here.

“Do I think that we’re in the end times? I don’t know, and I think that it’s probably bad for me spiritually to focus too much on it because there are like things you got to do. I got to be good to my wife. I got to be good to my kids. I have to be, you know, as good of a leader as I can for the United States of America,” Vance replied.
“I think that there are, like, things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the Antichrist was, was walking among us. But again, I try not to focus too much on it,” he said.

“While I wouldn’t be shocked if we are living in the end times, what I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now, and if that leads to the end times, okay,” Vance said.

The vice president, who like President Donald Trump has been a proponent of building data centers to support AI development, pointed to some uses of AI as having “really, really weird spiritual dark energy.”

Referring to a friend with a spouse who was using AI for marriage counseling, Vance said, “there’s no real human feedback. It sort of short circuits that social part of our brain where we respond to other people’s wants and needs, and just completely — like I think that’s kind of satanic.”

Asked to rate on a scale of 1 to 10 his chances of getting into heaven, Vance said, “That is a tough question. It’s high, but it’s not 10, right? I mean, it’s it’s it’s a it’s a seven or it’s an eight. Like I’m always one of these people who is is always going to have little doubts. And like, if you’d asked me that question a year ago, probably was like a five or a six.”

Crawford asked Vance if he’d come across any evidence the spiritual world is real since becoming VP. “I don’t have the the file that says, oh, this wasn’t a UFO; it was actually a demon,” Vance said, and “I don’t have like a top secret file that sort of proves that one way or the other.”
He said he did see something before he became vice president — Trump surviving an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in 2024.
“He points to a chart, just so happens to be at the exact moment that the guy took a shot. Now, again, there is a physical explanation for that,” Vance said.

“He turned his head. The guy fired the bullet. Crazy coincidence, right? These things happen. But I think that that’s a very spiritually impoverished way to look at things. Like whatever the reason is, whatever God was trying to accomplish, like it is just so obvious to me that coincidences like that don’t happen without the hand of providence.”
Had Trump not survived, Vance said, he would have viewed it as part of a “broader conspiracy.”

“I would have assumed very dark forces had taken out Donald Trump, right as he was about to come back into the White House,” Vance said. “There would have just been an illegitimacy to our entire political system.”

Crawford asked Vance about Trump’s post on social media of an AI-generated image of himself as Jesus earlier this year, which Crawford said offended him. Trump initially contended he thought the image was of him as a doctor, then took down the post amid widespread criticism from even some of his own backers.

Vance defended the president. “He did not mean to, like, mock or mimic God, that’s just not who he is,” Vance said, adding that the president often tries to keep things light and constantly makes jokes. “He’s a bit of a ballbuster, for those of us who work with him, and he just likes to have a good time. And I think that if people appreciated that, they would recognize, he’s not trying to offend people, he’s trying to keep things light,” he said.

title: DOJ sues Kansas school district over transgender student guidelines and parental consent
summary: In what it called “a first-of-its-kind lawsuit,” the Justice Department has sued a school district in Kansas over its guidelines on student gender identity and assisting transgender students.
story: In what it called “a first-of-its-kind lawsuit,” the Justice Department has sued a school district in Kansas over its guidelines on student gender identity and assisting transgender students.
The lawsuit, filed Monday, is the latest escalation from the Trump administration targeting school districts for policies or guidelines to accommodate transgender students in academic settings.

The Justice Department said it was seeking to stop the Kansas City, Kansas, public school district from violating federal law by “facilitating secret ‘gender transitions’ for children at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent.”

“Parental rights are paramount in the operation of America’s public schools, and Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools does not know children better than their own parents,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, said in a statement. “The Department will not tolerate school districts playing fast and loose with federal law in the service of radical gender ideology.”

The complaint says district guidelines violated the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA), which allow parents to view students’ educational records and threaten loss of federal funding for failing to comply.

The district is at risk of losing nearly $70 million in federal funding if it is found teachers or administrators withheld information related to a student’s gender identity, NBC News affiliate KSHB 41 reports.

According to the Justice Department complaint, the Kansas City district’s guidance says that a student or their parents should contact the school if a student is transgender or gender nonconforming and is seeking any related accommodations.

“If any staff member learns a student is transgender or gender non-conforming, that information should be relayed to the school principal without delay,” the guideline says, according to the complaint. “The school principal should discuss available accommodations and resources with the student or the student’s parent or legal guardian, including the availability of a planning meeting. If it becomes known that the student does not want the student’s parent or legal guardian included at this stage, that request will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.”

The guidelines say those requests will be evaluated by the executive director of Student Services & Family Support, the director of Student Support Programs, the executive director of Equity and Inclusion and the district’s attorney.

“When reviewing the request, the district will consider the student’s age, the student’s grade level, the student’s welfare based on the information available to the district at that time, and any other relevant information,” the guidelines say, according to the complaint.
The school district’s guidance also says that upon request, administrators will schedule a planning meeting to discuss a student’s preferred pronoun use and restroom and locker use.
The district for 21,000 students said in a statement to KSHB this week that it’s been in full cooperation with federal law and is “disappointed by the DOJ’s decision to file the lawsuit.”
Because the matter is now pending in federal court, district leaders said they would respond to the complaint through the appropriate legal channel and not issue additional public comments.

After the Justice Department threatened to sue the district in late July, KCKPS Superintendent Anna ‌Stubblefield told KSHB 41 that she could not recall an incident in which the district withheld such information from parents.

“It also is not policy, it is guidance,” Stubblefield said. “There’s nowhere in the guidance where we say ‘withhold information from parents.’ We have no reason or incentive to withhold information from parents about anything that they’re entitled to for their students.”
The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department in April said it determined that four school districts in Kansas were in violation of the Family Education Rights and Privacy Act.
The Trump administration has previously threatened to cut federal funding from school districts over policies regarding transgender students and gender identity, including in Maryland and Michigan.

In March, the Supreme Court barred California from enforcing state rules that restrict when schools can notify parents about students who come out as transgender and require teachers to use children’s preferred pronouns.
Lawyers for the state had argued that the policies were not as broad as the plaintiffs suggested.

“Currently, under California’s laws and constitutional provisions on privacy and antidiscrimination, schools may balance parental interests with students’ particular needs and circumstances, such as the risk of harm upon disclosure of the student’s gender identity without student consent,” they wrote at the time.
The rules “allow disclosure to parents in some circumstances and limit disclosure in others,” the lawyers said.

title: Arizona congressman heard ‘freight train crash’ sound during Grand Canyon flash flood
summary: Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.
story: Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.
Schweikert told NBC News from his office in Washington on Tuesday that the loud crash was followed by a powerful stream of mud and debris-filled water.

Two visitors died and another is still missing after flash flooding from a sudden deluge of rain briefly transformed Bright Angel Creek into a full-fledged river. About 80 people were evacuated from campsites around the historic Phantom Ranch area of the park.

The retiring member of Congress and the rest of his group were about 100 yards away from the danger zone without cellphone service. His guide led the group to an area off the Colorado River near Bright Angel Creek.
They later left the area on foot — traveling on higher ground — and camped for the night nearby.

It is “monsoon season” in Arizona, but Schweikert said there was not more than a drizzle of precipitation where he was when the dangerous flood ripped through, underscoring the potential randomness of such events.
“At some point, you realized this is a big deal; something’s really gone haywire. ... It was a ginormous flash flood,” he said.
The intricate terrain of the Grand Canyon can invite the type of deadly flood conditions that hit the southern part of the national park over the weekend.
“The deluge downpour could have been miles away and was channeled into the canyon, and what used to be a creek now is a river,” said Schweikert, who is a regular Grand Canyon hiker.
The water supply system for the park was also severely damaged, along with part of a new $208 million water pipeline project that was underway near the ranch.
Schweikert said he would likely be involved in working to get the damage addressed once proper assessments are made. “Right now, the heartbreak is a couple of people lost their lives,” he added.

He also cautioned visitors to the park to carefully monitor the weather and to use extreme caution if storms are expected in the vicinity at all. If storms are nearby, hikes through narrow passages known as slot canyons should be strictly avoided because of the risk of getting trapped, the seasoned adventurer said.
“It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Schweikert said.

title: Anger over planned AI data center drives Missouri city’s voters to recall council member
summary: Voters in Independence, Missouri, voted to recall a city council member over his decision in March to back billions of dollars in tax breaks for an AI data center.
story: Voters in Independence, Missouri, on Tuesday night voted to recall a City Council member who has served for more than a decade, rebuking his decision in March to back billions of dollars in tax breaks for a proposed AI data center.
The recall effort comes amid escalating backlash nationwide against the rapid proliferation of data centers that is influencing federal and local races ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Independence City Councilmember John Perkins was recalled Tuesday, with nearly 70% of his district voting to remove him, according to unofficial election results from Jackson County.
The anger in Independence, a Kansas City suburb with 121,000 residents, over the construction of the artificial intelligence data center on the city’s eastern flank has been mounting for months.
In March, Perkins was one of five council members who voted to issue tax breaks totaling more than $6 billion to Dutch company Nebius for the construction of the planned $150 billion data center.

More than 50 community members attended and spoke at the City Council meeting in which the tax breaks were approved. A local chapter of the progressive Sunrise Movement organized a letter-writing campaign ahead of the meeting for community members to oppose the tax breaks in an attempt to sink the data center project.

A Facebook group for Independence residents who oppose the data center called Stop the AI Data Center in Independence has  115,000 members, many who celebrated Tuesday night when the unofficial election results showed Perkins had been recalled.

“Politicians aren’t entitled to elected positions. They’re elected by the people to serve those people. When they stop serving the people they were elected to represent, they’re voted out of office,” one member of the group wrote Tuesday. “This is democracy in action.”
Another member of the group described speaking with Perkins outside their polling place Tuesday, writing that they’d told him, “Enjoy the consequences of selling us out to the data center.”

Perkins has not yet responded to a request for comment on the recall election. But in a recent Kansas City Star op-ed, he urged voters to judge him by his full record, adding that he stood by the data center vote.

“You can disagree with that call, and I respect that,” Perkins wrote. “However, disagreement isn’t a crime, and I don’t believe it is grounds to attempt to overturn an election that happened two years ago.”

Two other City Council members who’d voted in favor of the data center tax breaks — Bridget McCandless and Jared Fears — lost their subsequent election bids in April. Fears was running for re-election to the council and McCandless was running for mayor.
Opposition to AI data centers has surfaced in communities around the country, looming over the coming midterms and prompting candidates to choose sides.

For some Republicans, that has meant opposing President Donald Trump, who recently signaled strong support for data centers — writing on Truth Social that communities that oppose them “want to end up being backwards and poor.”

title: Lindsay Clancy jury tells judge they’re still deadlocked on 5th day of deliberations
summary: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial told the judge on Wednesday they were deadlocked for a second time, a day after they issued a first deadlock note to the judge.
story: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial told the judge on Wednesday they were deadlocked for a second time, a day after they issued a first deadlock note to the judge.

Judge William Sullivan sent the jury back for a fifth day of deliberations on Wednesday morning, after they were dismissed around 3:30 p.m. on Tuesday. When the jury came back from lunch at 2:00 p.m. on Wednesday, they submitted a note to Sullivan that they were still deadlocked.

After Wednesday’s deadlock note, Sullivan read the jury the Tuey-Rodriguez instructions, which essentially asks them to give deliberations one last chance and tells jurors that it’s “desirable” they reach a verdict.

“You should consider that it is desirable that the case be decided,” the instructions say. “You should consider that you have been selected in the same manner, and from the same source, as any future jury would be.”

According to Massachusetts law, a judge can only ask a jury to keep deliberating twice, unless the jury consents to further deliberations. If the jury still cannot reach a unanimous verdict after the third deadlock, the judge can declare a mistrial.

Tuesday was the first time the public got a glimpse into the jury’s thinking. After just about an hour of deliberations, the group of nine women and three men returned to the courtroom to alert Sullivan that there had so far been no unanimous decision reached among them.
Sullivan sent the jury back to the deliberation room and encouraged them to reach a verdict. They deliberated for another seven hours on Wednesday before again stating they were deadlocked.
Add to Google
Add to Google
The judge kicked off court Wednesday by appearing to speak briefly to each of the 12 jurors — and alternate jurors — individually in a sidebar before sending them out for deliberations.
It was not immediately clear what Sullivan asked each of the jurors, but he said he asked them each one question.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington spoke to reporters outside of court Wednesday morning, and called the jury “incredibly hardworking.”
Later Wednesday, while the court was on recess for lunch, Reddington added, “The time they’ve put into this so far is unbelievable.”

When asked how long he expects it will be before a verdict is returned, Reddington said he didn’t know, but he said he did not have any concerns about a second trial, should this one end in a hung jury.
On Tuesday, Reddington told reporters that he would “absolutely” go to trial again.
The jury must decide whether Clancy is criminally responsible for killing her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — on Jan 24., 2023.

Clancy’s defense team has argued she was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations that night, a symptom of the postpartum psychosis they said she was experiencing at the time. She sought extensive mental health care, they said, but doctors failed her by overprescribing her medications.

The prosecution, though, has argued that Clancy was not actually in psychosis when she strangled her children with exercise bands and threw herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed and in a wheelchair. They said she planned the attacks ahead of time and purposefully sent her then-husband out of the home so she could carry out the killings.

While the prosecution has sought a first-degree murder conviction, which would carry a life sentence, the jury can also convict Clancy of lesser charges — second-degree murder or manslaughter — or deem her not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility.

Also on Tuesday, just after court was dismissed, Dawn Light, 56, from Sutton, Massachusetts, was arrested outside of the courthouse in Plymouth, a spokesperson for the Massachusetts state police confirmed. The state police said there was no further information on the arrest at this time.
Light was arraigned Wednesday on one charge of aggravated intimidation of jurors, witnesses, police or court officials.

She pleaded not guilty and claimed that she was not taking photos and videos outside of court, rather, she was waiting for Clancy to exit so she could wave to the defendant. But when officials asked to look through Light’s phone, they found photos and videos of people — including jurors — exiting the courthouse Tuesday.
Light’s defense attorney claimed she was trying to get a photo of Clancy. It was a “complete misunderstanding,” her lawyer said Wednesday, and Light has the “utmost respect” for the judicial process.

The judge did not impose bail, but said Light must stay away from the courthouse, court grounds, and any jurors and witnesses. Light must also refrain from disseminating or producing any photos that may be on her iCloud account in relation to the incident.

title: Tiger Woods pleads ‘no contest’ in DUI case
summary: Tiger Woods reached a plea deal with prosecutors Wednesday in connection with DUI charges against him following a crash near his Florida home earlier this year.
story: MARTIN COUNTY, Florida — Tiger Woods reached a plea deal with prosecutors Wednesday in connection with DUI charges against him, following a car crash near his Florida home earlier this year.

Woods, 50, appeared in a Martin County courtroom and pleaded no contest to a reduced charge of reckless driving and refusal to submit to a lawful test, avoiding time in prison. The troubled golfer also agreed to have his driving license suspended for five years and fined $1,500.

In March, Woods was involved in a rollover on Jupiter Island, just north of Palm Beach, Florida. He initially pleaded not guilty to two charges — driving under the influence and refusing to submit to testing —  in connection with the crash.

Had he fought the charges and been convicted, Woods could have faced up to a year in county jail, according to prosecutors. A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt but means the accused will offer no defense. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system.
Woods’ attorney declined to comment. The golf champion later left the courthouse without addressing reporters.
Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl addressed reporters after the hearing.

“Of all the people in the world who should not get behind the wheel of the car, it’s the gentleman who is one of the most recognizable faces on the planet,” Bakkedahl said. “Somebody will see him, whether it’s in Georgia or Nevada or New York or where have you. He’s not to drive a car.”
Bakkedahl said he was unsure if the golf champion would be allowed to drive a golf cart under the terms of the deal.
Woods arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law. She sat behind him during the hearing.
The March crash involved a dark Land Rover that Woods had been driving and a truck carrying a trailer, according to officials.
At the time, the driver of the truck said he was starting to turn into a driveway off a two-lane road when he looked into his mirror and saw Woods driving “at high speeds.”
The driver tried veering off the road, but Woods’ Land Rover “overtook” the truck at the last minute, swerving to avoid a crash, officials said. Woods ultimately clipped the back of the trailer.
Woods’ SUV rolled onto the driver’s side door, according to officials, leaving the golfer to exit by climbing out of the window.
Neither Woods nor the truck driver was injured in the crash.
Woods told authorities that he was under the influence and had two hydrocodone pills in his pocket upon his arrest, Bakkedahl said.
In the days following the incident, Woods said in a statement on social media that he was seeking treatment. “I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in,” he wrote.
Bakkedahl described Woods and his attorney as being cooperative in handing over evidence to officials.
Several days before the crash, Woods played in a match in the finals for Tomorrow’s Golf League. His team, Jupiter Links Golf Club, lost to the Los Angeles Golf Club in the competition.
Woods, who is among the most influential figures in golf, has been involved in several road incidents in recent years.
In 2021, he was involved in a rollover in Southern California but did not face criminal charges.
The golf champion was also arrested and charged with a DUI in Florida in 2017. He checked himself into a clinic that same year.

title: Ariana Grande tearfully ends 41-show tour and steps back from public life
summary: A teary and visibly emotional Ariana Grande bid farewell to her fans as her 41 show tour concluded in London and she began her planned withdrawal from public life.
story: LONDON — A teary and visibly emotional Ariana Grande bid a temporary farewell to her fans as her 41-show “Eternal Sunshine Tour” concluded in London on Tuesday night, kickstarting her planned withdrawal from public life.
Addressing the audience in London’s famed O2 arena, the pop singer said she was “grateful” to her fans for making her show “so special.”

“This has been one of the most beautiful, extraordinary experiences of my life,” Grande said, dressed in black and perched on a stool on stage. “I just wanted to express my gratitude without sobbing completely.”
“I’ll cherish this experience always,” she added.

Grande, known for hits including “thank you, next” and “hate that i made you love me,” made global headlines in August when she said she would be taking a “step back from visibility” following “public scrutiny.”
The announcement came after the release of her latest music video, “petal,” which reignited a public debate about her health.

Representatives for Grande said last month that she was looking forward to finishing her tour “on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.”
Grande concluded her tour in knee-high boots rather than her signature heels after stating she was “bandaged up underneath” following a “deep cut” on her foot, which she called a “minor injury.”
Add to Google
Add to Google

Grande’s “Eternal Sunshine Tour,” which promoted the 2024 album of the same name, began in Oakland, California, in June. She previously labeled the shows “one last hurrah” and has expressed her desire to take on more acting roles.
Grande was nominated for an Oscar for her performance as Glinda in the hit musical movie “Wicked.”
She had been set to reunite with “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey in a revival of Stephen Sondheim’s “Sunday in the Park With George,” in London next summer, before she pulled out last month.
In a statement Tuesday on Instagram, Bailey said he has also decided to “step back” from the Sondheim show. He added that “Ari is one of my dearest friends, and my support for her is unwavering.”

title: Healthcare tops the Democrats’ to-do list if they win control of the House in 2026
summary: Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said his party would unify around undoing Trump’s Medicaid cuts and reviving ACA funds that the GOP ended. Some Democrats want to go bigger.
story: WASHINGTON — Vying to become House speaker in a few months, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries outlined four items on the agenda that he said would enjoy “uniform Democratic support” and advance the party’s goal of “making life more affordable.”
The first two were about healthcare, and all four set a direct contrast with President Donald Trump.

“We have to reverse the Medicaid cuts. We should extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits,” Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Monday in response to a question from NBC News. “We should restore congressional authority as it relates to tariffs, because the Trump tariffs are making life more expensive for the American people. And we should end, decisively, if it’s still going on, Donald Trump’s reckless and costly war of choice in the Middle East.”
Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said there is consensus that Democrats’ first bill out of the gate, legislation that carries high symbolic weight known as H.R. 1, would need to focus on affordability.
But there’s not yet consensus on what the bill would look like, as voters cite the cost of living as a top concern heading into November’s elections.
Beyer argued that the best way to tackle the topic would be to restore hundreds of billions of dollars in Medicaid and the ACA subsidies that were cut in Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill.”
“In the affordability debate, nothing’s more central to it than healthcare,” Beyer said in an interview. “My expectation is that it’ll very much be about affordability one way or the other.”

Jeffries said there are “a whole host of things” still to work on, saying, “We’ve established five working groups on affordability” — on housing, healthcare, childcare, groceries and food, and gas and utilities.
He added that Democrats would also conduct aggressive oversight of the Trump administration and “certainly will fight to hold the crooks accountable.”

Jeffries’ agenda for a possible majority reflects an emerging consensus among many Democrats across the party spectrum, who said healthcare should top the party’s legislative to-do list in 2027. The lowest-hanging fruits are restoring Trump’s Medicaid cuts, which no Democrats voted for, and reviving the expired ACA, or “Obamacare,” tax credits, which every Democrat wanted to extend last year before Republicans blocked them, leading to coverage losses and substantially higher premiums for millions.
Still, many Democrats say reversing Trump on Medicaid and the ACA would be the bare minimum — and want the party to do much more on healthcare.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said it would “absolutely not” be enough to simply restore Medicaid and ACA funds.

“Of course, we need to take immediate action on those ACA subsidies and making sure that we lower those prices immediately. But it doesn’t fix the deeper systemic issue that has led healthcare to be one of the primary drivers of inflationary costs over the last decade, frankly,” she said in an interview.

“We need to be doing a lot more to take on corporate power, to break up a lot of these monopolies that are rolling up — Big Pharma, insurance, private equity entering the space of healthcare unchecked,” she added. “I think there’s a lot here for us to really dig in on, to work on.”

While there’s agreement on restoring the Medicaid and ACA funds that were undone by Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, there are divisions inside the Democratic Party about what its own healthcare agenda should be.

Ocasio-Cortez is part of a large and influential faction on the left that wants to pursue a “Medicare for All” system that would diminish — if not abolish — private insurance and give the government power to negotiate prices of medication and services downward. Many moderate Democrats have rejected that idea in favor of less disruptive changes, although the center-left hasn’t coalesced around a preferred vision. One outside center-left group floated “free primary care for all” as a way to break the stalemate between supporters of a single-payer Medicare for All system and of focusing on building on the current ACA.
In June, Jeffries tapped Ocasio-Cortez and Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to lead the health care working group for the caucus, according to a letter he wrote to lawmakers that was obtained by NBC News.

Part of what House Democrats would do next year depends on the size of their majority, should they win. If it’s a narrow majority of a handful of seats, as the House has operated in since 2021 under either party, they might be limited to the lowest common denominator and blocked from doing anything too aggressive on healthcare or any other major issues.
Jeffries, who is politically cautious by nature, is leery of getting ahead of his conference and overpromising without knowing what kind of majority he’d have.

A source familiar with Jeffries’ thinking said Democrats plan to take action in three tranches: the first 100 hours, when they would focus on urgent priorities with party consensus to provide relief for Americans; then the first 100 days, to build on that foundation with more aggressive efforts to lower costs alongside investigative moves; and then the first year.
Rep. Jared Moskowitz of Florida, a moderate Democrat in a competitive district, said the Medicaid and ACA plans may not be “a complete agenda” but backed those positions as a good place to start.

“Let’s talk about what we can get done quickly to provide the American people economic relief,” Moskowitz said. “You know we need 60 votes in the Senate for any piece of legislation, and then we need the president to sign it.”

Democrats have consistently enjoyed an issue advantage on healthcare since 2018, the last time they captured the House. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that Americans trust Democrats over Republicans to handle healthcare by 38% to 25%.

Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., who is poised to chair the Budget Committee if Democrats flip the House, also said he would be focused in the new year on “reversing the damage” to healthcare from Trump’s megabill.

“Keep in mind that when we take over in January, we will literally just be one month into the Medicaid cuts’ taking effect. That’s the biggest bulk by far of their healthcare cuts and where millions more people are going to lose their healthcare,” Boyle said in an interview. “So from the Budget Committee perspective, that’s what I’m focused on.”
Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, a member of the Appropriations and Budget committees, said she wants the party to take a much broader, more ambitious approach.

She said she is proud of the work House Democrats did on President Joe Biden’s Build Back Better agenda, which died in the Senate because of opposition from moderate Joe Manchin of West Virginia, who is no longer in office. Escobar said she would want to pursue much of that framework in Democrats’ first bill, including paid family and medical leave, universal prekindergarten, childcare subsidies and ACA subsidies, as well as student loan forgiveness.

“I would want to go big. My constituents and Americans all over the country are really hurting — it is so profound. And the increase in utility bills has been so overwhelming. I have constituents in my district who are paying more for their utility bills than their mortgage, and so people are really suffering right now. And my view is we have to offer the solutions that they deserve and they need, and we’ve done it before,” Escobar told NBC News.
“There is a way to message it. Obviously, the bigger it is, the more challenging that is,” she added.
But, she said, “there would be one central theme: bring down the costs that are making your life difficult.”

For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend.

title: DOJ sues Kansas school district over transgender student guidelines and parental consent
summary: In what it called “a first-of-its-kind lawsuit,” the Justice Department has sued a school district in Kansas over its guidelines on student gender identity and assisting transgender students.
story: In what it called “a first-of-its-kind lawsuit,” the Justice Department has sued a school district in Kansas over its guidelines on student gender identity and assisting transgender students.
The lawsuit, filed Monday, is the latest escalation from the Trump administration targeting school districts for policies or guidelines to accommodate transgender students in academic settings.

The Justice Department said it was seeking to stop the Kansas City, Kansas, public school district from violating federal law by “facilitating secret ‘gender transitions’ for children at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent.”

“Parental rights are paramount in the operation of America’s public schools, and Kansas City, Kansas Public Schools does not know children better than their own parents,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, said in a statement. “The Department will not tolerate school districts playing fast and loose with federal law in the service of radical gender ideology.”

The complaint says district guidelines violated the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA), which allow parents to view students’ educational records and threaten loss of federal funding for failing to comply.

The district is at risk of losing nearly $70 million in federal funding if it is found teachers or administrators withheld information related to a student’s gender identity, NBC News affiliate KSHB 41 reports.

According to the Justice Department complaint, the Kansas City district’s guidance says that a student or their parents should contact the school if a student is transgender or gender nonconforming and is seeking any related accommodations.

“If any staff member learns a student is transgender or gender non-conforming, that information should be relayed to the school principal without delay,” the guideline says, according to the complaint. “The school principal should discuss available accommodations and resources with the student or the student’s parent or legal guardian, including the availability of a planning meeting. If it becomes known that the student does not want the student’s parent or legal guardian included at this stage, that request will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.”

The guidelines say those requests will be evaluated by the executive director of Student Services & Family Support, the director of Student Support Programs, the executive director of Equity and Inclusion and the district’s attorney.

“When reviewing the request, the district will consider the student’s age, the student’s grade level, the student’s welfare based on the information available to the district at that time, and any other relevant information,” the guidelines say, according to the complaint.
The school district’s guidance also says that upon request, administrators will schedule a planning meeting to discuss a student’s preferred pronoun use and restroom and locker use.
The district for 21,000 students said in a statement to KSHB this week that it’s been in full cooperation with federal law and is “disappointed by the DOJ’s decision to file the lawsuit.”
Because the matter is now pending in federal court, district leaders said they would respond to the complaint through the appropriate legal channel and not issue additional public comments.

After the Justice Department threatened to sue the district in late July, KCKPS Superintendent Anna ‌Stubblefield told KSHB 41 that she could not recall an incident in which the district withheld such information from parents.

“It also is not policy, it is guidance,” Stubblefield said. “There’s nowhere in the guidance where we say ‘withhold information from parents.’ We have no reason or incentive to withhold information from parents about anything that they’re entitled to for their students.”
The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department in April said it determined that four school districts in Kansas were in violation of the Family Education Rights and Privacy Act.
The Trump administration has previously threatened to cut federal funding from school districts over policies regarding transgender students and gender identity, including in Maryland and Michigan.

In March, the Supreme Court barred California from enforcing state rules that restrict when schools can notify parents about students who come out as transgender and require teachers to use children’s preferred pronouns.
Lawyers for the state had argued that the policies were not as broad as the plaintiffs suggested.

“Currently, under California’s laws and constitutional provisions on privacy and antidiscrimination, schools may balance parental interests with students’ particular needs and circumstances, such as the risk of harm upon disclosure of the student’s gender identity without student consent,” they wrote at the time.
The rules “allow disclosure to parents in some circumstances and limit disclosure in others,” the lawyers said.

title: Tiger Woods pleads ‘no contest’ in DUI case
summary: Tiger Woods reached a plea deal with prosecutors Wednesday in connection with DUI charges against him following a crash near his Florida home earlier this year.
story: MARTIN COUNTY, Florida — Tiger Woods reached a plea deal with prosecutors Wednesday in connection with DUI charges against him, following a car crash near his Florida home earlier this year.

Woods, 50, appeared in a Martin County courtroom and pleaded no contest to a reduced charge of reckless driving and refusal to submit to a lawful test, avoiding time in prison. The troubled golfer also agreed to have his driving license suspended for five years and fined $1,500.

In March, Woods was involved in a rollover on Jupiter Island, just north of Palm Beach, Florida. He initially pleaded not guilty to two charges — driving under the influence and refusing to submit to testing —  in connection with the crash.

Had he fought the charges and been convicted, Woods could have faced up to a year in county jail, according to prosecutors. A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt but means the accused will offer no defense. The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system.
Woods’ attorney declined to comment. The golf champion later left the courthouse without addressing reporters.
Martin County State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl addressed reporters after the hearing.

“Of all the people in the world who should not get behind the wheel of the car, it’s the gentleman who is one of the most recognizable faces on the planet,” Bakkedahl said. “Somebody will see him, whether it’s in Georgia or Nevada or New York or where have you. He’s not to drive a car.”
Bakkedahl said he was unsure if the golf champion would be allowed to drive a golf cart under the terms of the deal.
Woods arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, President Donald Trump’s former daughter-in-law. She sat behind him during the hearing.
The March crash involved a dark Land Rover that Woods had been driving and a truck carrying a trailer, according to officials.
At the time, the driver of the truck said he was starting to turn into a driveway off a two-lane road when he looked into his mirror and saw Woods driving “at high speeds.”
The driver tried veering off the road, but Woods’ Land Rover “overtook” the truck at the last minute, swerving to avoid a crash, officials said. Woods ultimately clipped the back of the trailer.
Woods’ SUV rolled onto the driver’s side door, according to officials, leaving the golfer to exit by climbing out of the window.
Neither Woods nor the truck driver was injured in the crash.
Woods told authorities that he was under the influence and had two hydrocodone pills in his pocket upon his arrest, Bakkedahl said.
In the days following the incident, Woods said in a statement on social media that he was seeking treatment. “I know and understand the seriousness of the situation I find myself in,” he wrote.
Bakkedahl described Woods and his attorney as being cooperative in handing over evidence to officials.
Several days before the crash, Woods played in a match in the finals for Tomorrow’s Golf League. His team, Jupiter Links Golf Club, lost to the Los Angeles Golf Club in the competition.
Woods, who is among the most influential figures in golf, has been involved in several road incidents in recent years.
In 2021, he was involved in a rollover in Southern California but did not face criminal charges.
The golf champion was also arrested and charged with a DUI in Florida in 2017. He checked himself into a clinic that same year.

title: Student who felt ‘humiliated’ by ICE ankle monitor dies by suicide
summary: Pierre Damas Bel, 20, expressed feeling “shame and humiliation” at having to wear by an ankle monitor. The college student died by suicide days later.
story: Hours before Ohio college student and athlete Pierre Damas Bel took his own life Monday morning, he called his father for help.

It was around 8 a.m., and he was sitting inside his car on the side of Interstate 70, struggling mentally and emotionally with the shame of being forced to wear an ankle monitor by immigration officials. Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian student at Wright State University, said he had been bullied at school and felt “humiliated” by the device.
“I told him to come home so we can talk,” Bel’s father said in an emailed statement. “Around 11 the police showed at my door to report that my son threw himself under a truck.”
Bel stepped into oncoming traffic and died from his injuries, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said. His family blamed the humiliation brought on by the ankle monitor he had been wearing since July.
Carl Ruby, a local pastor and immigration advocate, said in a statement that Bel’s family wanted people to know it was a suicide related to immigration policies.

Bel arrived in the U.S. in 2024 and applied for admission into the country using the now-defunct CBP One app, Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in an emailed statement. He was released into the country and settled in Springfield with his parents and two brothers.

Bel excelled in academics and athletics, becoming an honor roll student at Springfield High School and joining JROTC. He was recruited to play soccer at Wittenberg University and hoped to attend medical school after college, immigration advocates said.

In May, the Springfield City School District featured Bel in a Facebook post highlighting recipients of a local scholarship that offered $2,500 to each student. Bel wore a blue suit and a black bow tie as he accepted his award, with a big smile on his face.
The future seemed bright.
Things began to change July 29, when ICE placed him in an “alternatives to detention program” with an ankle monitor while he continued his immigration proceedings.
He documented the experience on social media, writing July 30 that he came to the country to study, not “commit a crime or hurt anyone.”
“Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote.

Bel was one of the roughly 300,000 Haitian nationals living in the U.S. who lost their temporary protected status, or TPS, at the end of July following a Supreme Court decision. The policy change triggered a wave of fear and confusion in Springfield, where 12,000 Haitians live.
ICE said it does not comment on the cause of death while an investigation is pending.
“We will not speculate about unverified claims regarding other individuals,” it said in an emailed statement.

According to the Wittenberg University men’s soccer team, Bel was no longer able to play for the team after he lost TPS. He transferred to nearby Wright State University and immediately faced taunts and bullying from students, his family said.
“We do not want to politicize this, but this is a political problem, and the only solution is a political solution,” Ruby told reporters Tuesday.
“The only way that this will never be correct is if Republican elected officials join us in demanding better policy,” he said.
Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, has criticized the Trump administration’s harsh immigration enforcement and its impact on Ohio residents.
On Tuesday, he called Bel’s suicide a “horrible tragedy” that never should have happened.
“I think we have to ask ourselves: Is this really good? Is it what we want done to people like this being picked up and facing deportation? Do we want that being done in our name?” he told reporters.
Springfield, a small city in southwestern Ohio, became the center of salacious and unfounded rumors about the Haitian community during the 2024 presidential election.

In August, ICE began alerting Haitians to appear in person at check-ins, where they were given ankle monitors to track their whereabouts until immigration judges can decide whether they may have legitimate reasons to remain in the country, such as asylum claims.

Ankle monitors are usually issued because of a lack of detention space for more than 300,000 Haitians who lost TPS after the Supreme Court decision in June, a senior Department of Homeland Security official has said.

Some Springfield residents saw the arrival of Haitian nationals as a driving force behind the city’s economic renaissance. Others complained that Springfield was not prepared to welcome so many immigrants, who contributed to long waits at clinics and were driving up rental prices. Despite the unwanted attention, many Haitian residents thrived in their adopted home, taking jobs in manufacturing, buying homes and opening businesses.
Occasionally tensions boiled over. White supremacist groups and alt-right influencers have clashed with local immigration advocates and faith leaders who sought to protect the Haitian community.

Viles Dorsainvil, co-founder and executive director of the Haitian Support Center, said the Bel family is one of several hundred who have poured into the center seeking legal help and guidance. He estimates 34 people have been detained since TPS ended.
Bel’s is believed to be the first suicide in Springfield related to immigration enforcement, he said.
“I know many folks are depressed right now,” Dorsainvil said. “I never had in my mind that it would have gotten to that point.”

If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

title: Judge rules that the trial of Tyler Robinson in Charlie Kirk’s killing can go forward
summary: A judge in Utah is expected to decide whether there is enough evidence to move forward with a trial against the man accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk.
story: A judge in Utah on Tuesday ruled that a trial for the 23-year-old man accused of fatally shooting prominent conservative political activist Charlie Kirk can move forward.

District Judge Tony Graf issued the decision after a day of arguments in a probable cause hearing. Prosecutors argued there was enough evidence against Tyler Robinson to proceed with the case, while defense attorneys maintained that the evidence was insufficient.
“It is hereby ordered that the defendant, Tyler James Robinson, is bound over for trial,” Graf said.
Robinson’s defense attorney then entered pleas of not guilty on all counts on his behalf. The next court date was set for Oct. 23.
Prosecutors have charged Robinson with aggravated murder, a first-degree felony that makes him eligible for the death penalty, and other counts.

Robinson is accused of killing Kirk with a single rifle round fired from a rooftop at an event at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10. The assassination of Kirk, the 31-year-old co-founder of the youth advocacy group Turning Point USA and a close ally of President Donald Trump, rocked U.S. politics.
In the lead-up to his ruling, Graf allowed lawyers on both sides to present closing arguments Tuesday.
“It’s not difficult to understand the motive here,” Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court. “The defendant’s views were repugnant to the positions that Charlie Kirk famously took.”
McBride alleged that Robinson threatened the lives of the people who attended Kirk’s event last September.
“You can’t shoot a rifle into a crowd of 3,000 people without knowing that you create a great risk of death to all those around your target,” McBride said in part.
Robinson’s defense attorney, Richard Novak, said the state cannot prove what would have motivated the shooting.
“There’s no evidence as to really what was in Mr. Robinson’s mind, if in fact he was the shooter, about Charlie Kirk,” Novak said.
“Because we have no testimony that Mr. Robinson had ever spoken about Charlie Kirk, that he’d ever heard anything he’d said, that he’d ever discussed anything” about Kirk in the past, Novak said.

Staci Visser, another defense attorney, argued that Utah’s legal aggravator, a circumstance that can support a harsher sentence, does not apply because Robinson is not accused of firing multiple shots or making threats.
“There is one act, there is one shot, there is one bullet, there is one victim,” she said.
Graf, in his ruling, allowed the aggravator and said the state met its burden at this preliminary stage, though he did not rule on the merits.

Tuesday’s high-stakes hearing came nearly two months after prosecutors laid out a detailed public reconstruction of the alleged events surrounding Kirk’s killing and presented a trove of evidence against Robinson, including security video, digital records and forensic material.

David Hull, a former State Bureau of Investigation agent, characterized Robinson’s alleged movements before and after the assassination. Hull’s testimony at a five-day hearing was accompanied by excerpts from campus video shown in court for the first time.

Robinson arrived at the university hours before the shooting, bought a meal from a campus Chick-fil-A restaurant, and made contact with representatives for Turning Point USA, Hull testified. Robinson then changed outfits and took a position on a rooftop overlooking the amphitheater where Kirk was speaking, Hull said.

In a video shown in court July 7, Robinson could be seen crouching on the rooftop, Hull told the court. Then, after a bullet hit Kirk, Robinson could be seen darting across the roof, dropping to ground level and sprinting away on foot, Hull added.
Prosecutors played another video featuring partially redacted excerpts from law enforcement investigators’ interview with Lance Twiggs, Robinson’s former romantic partner and roommate.

The day after Kirk’s assassination, Twiggs told investigators, Robinson nervously paced their apartment and expressed regret. Twiggs told investigators that he asked Robinson whether it was true that he fatally shot Kirk.
In the emotional interaction that followed, according to Twiggs, Robinson “said he wishes he hadn’t done it.”
Twiggs told investigators that Robinson said he intended to confess to his parents or go to the police. He turned himself in to law enforcement authorities later that day.

Investigators have said they found the suspected murder weapon — a bolt-action rifle — wrapped in a towel in a wooded area near the Utah Valley University amphitheater. DNA from both Robinson and Twiggs was on the towel, Sgt. Jennifer Faumuina of the Utah Department of Public Safety testified July 7.
Robinson’s lawyers tried to throw doubt on the DNA evidence and pressed a defense witness, FBI forensic analyst Amanda Bakker, about the potential for error in forensic testing and other issues.
Robinson’s defense lawyers have not provided an alternative theory for who killed Kirk.

In a charging document filed last September, prosecutors highlighted inscriptions alleged to have been etched on each round of the rifle, including the phrases “Hey Fascist! Catch!” and “If you Read This, You are GAY.”

Twiggs, in the recorded interview played in court, told investigators that Robinson never talked about Kirk before the shooting. The roommates-turned-partners had originally bonded over their shared love of video games, Twiggs said.
Kirk family attorney Jeffrey Neiman on Tuesday asked that the court act swiftly and to “set this trial as soon as practically possible.”
“The United States Constitution guarantees criminal defendants many rights. The right to delay is not among them,” Neiman said.
In a statement Tuesday night, Kirk’s family said Graf’s ruling “marks an important step in our family’s pursuit of justice for him.”

“Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie’s murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father,” Kirk’s family said. “We are grateful to all who have continued to pray for us, support us, and stand with us through a year of unimaginable grief.”

title: ‘Not the end of the movie’: Duane Davis’ lawyer on what’s next after Tupac murder verdict
summary: A day after Davis was found guilty of first-degree murder, his attorney told NBC News the defense had been preparing for an appeal before the trial even began.
story: A day after a Las Vegas jury found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of first-degree murder in the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, his attorney said the defense is looking toward its next fight, an appeal.

Davis, 63, was convicted Monday of first-degree murder with use of a deadly weapon in the fatal drive-by shooting of Shakur nearly 30 years ago. His sentencing is Oct. 13, when he faces the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison.

“We were preparing for the appeal, so even Mr. Davis knew that going in,” defense attorney Michael Sanft told NBC News on Tuesday. “Even before the first set of jurors came in for jury selection, we knew it was going to be an appeal issue.”

At the center of the appeal, Sanft said, will be the judge’s decision to allow jurors to hear statements Davis made to investigators under a 2008 proffer agreement. The agreement allowed him to speak candidly about what he did or witnessed that night in 1996 without facing charges.
The defense unsuccessfully sought to exclude the proffer statements before trial, because, Sanft said, “we believed it was highly prejudicial.”

Davis entered into the proffer agreement with federal investigators in 2008 as authorities investigated the killing of Christopher Wallace, the rapper known as the Notorious B.I.G. During those conversations, Davis provided investigators with information about Shakur’s killing.

Prosecutors in the case of Shakur’s killing, however, ultimately used Davis’ own words as a central part of their case against him, playing recordings of his statements to investigators and pointing jurors to accounts he later gave in interviews and his 2019 memoir, “Compton Street Legend.”

Sanft argued at trial that Davis had fabricated or embellished his accounts for money and notoriety and that investigators lacked physical evidence independently placing him at the scene of Shakur’s shooting.
Davis did not testify in his own defense, but jurors heard extensively from him through those earlier recordings and public statements.
Prosecutors called 24 witnesses in the 10-day trial. The defense called three witnesses.

Prosecutors portrayed Davis as a “shotcaller” in the South Side Compton Crips in California who helped orchestrate the attack on Shakur after Shakur and others beat Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’ nephew, inside the MGM Grand earlier that night.

Davis was not accused of firing the shots that killed Shakur. Prosecutors argued that he provided the gun and helped set the killing in motion. Under Nevada law, a person who aids or abets a murder can be held criminally responsible for the killing.

On Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was riding in a BMW driven by Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight near the Las Vegas Strip when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and someone inside opened fire.
Shakur, 25, was shot multiple times and died six days later. Knight survived.
For decades, no one was charged in the killing.

Davis became the only person ever prosecuted in connection with Shakur’s death after his public comments about the shooting helped revive investigators’ interest in the cold case. He is also the only person still alive who was believed to have been in the Cadillac when the shooting occurred. Sanft, however, said the defense continues to maintain that Davis was not in the car or in Las Vegas that night.
The jury rejected that defense, returning a unanimous guilty verdict after less than three hours of deliberations.
Sanft said the speed of the decision surprised him.

“For a jury to come back 2½ hours after submitting it to them ... they had pretty much made up their minds,” he said. “We thought for sure they were going to, you know, spend time over the night to come back in the morning and really get into the evidence.”
Sanft said Davis had been prepared for the possibility of a conviction because of the pretrial rulings.
“There was an understanding that there’s a long game being played here,” Sanft said. “That this was not the end of the movie, but rather just a phase.”
Sanft said the defense will seek the minimum possible sentence at Davis’ Oct. 13 sentencing, but he acknowledged that Davis could effectively spend the rest of his life behind bars.

“Mr. Davis is in his 60s. He’s in his mid-60s,” Sanft said. “You know, at this particular point, any sentence is potentially going to be a life sentence for him. So, of course, we’ll be asking for the minimum, but that’s not a good option right now for him.”
Despite the guilty verdict, Sanft said, Davis remains focused on what comes next.

“No one ever wants to lose, especially something like this,” he said. “But ultimately, at the end of the day, he understands that this is the next step. We have to take it before an appellate court. We have to go through that process, and then we come back at some point.”

title: Jason Kelce Says Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift Ditched This Wedding Tradition — and It Made It ‘So Fun’
summary: Travis Kelce and Jason Kelce discuss on “New Heights” what made Travis’s wedding to Taylor Swift such a success.
story: You may have heard that Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce got married at Madison Square Garden earlier this summer. What you may not have heard is how the event, which was attended by stars from all walks of life, went down.

In the Sept. 2 season premiere of Kelce’s “New Heights” podcast, which he hosts with brother Jason Kelce, the siblings opened up about that July 3 evening and the one tweak that made it even more of a success.

“The thing I really liked about this wedding in particular and the way you guys structured it was after all that was done, there wasn’t the sit-down formal stuff,” Jason Kelce said. “There wasn’t a bunch of the speeches. It was just time to party and have fun. And that’s what made it so fun to for me to be there.”
Guests were not allowed to have their phones, which changed the dynamics of the night.
“With no phones comes people not having to be on guard and like, feel that something, whatever that feeling is for everyone,” Travis Kelce said.

“It makes everyone be in the moment and be present. And it was so cool seeing everyone from my childhood not only mesh with Taylor and her childhood and her family and friends and people that she works with, to who we’ve come encounter with over our career and who we just admire as people and have become good friends with now.”
Travis Kelce, who said the night was something he and Swift “will never forget,” was also awed by hearing how the guests felt about the wedding.

“It’s just been so cool to see that world come together and hear through, person by person, after the wedding, just how awesome of a time everyone had there,” he said. “And that’s what we wanted it to be. We wanted it to be a beautiful ceremony, but we also wanted to make sure that everybody left there having some fun. And it was a magical night.”

The pair also had high praise for Adam Sandler, who officiated the nuptials. Travis Kelce said the comedian got ordained in New York and called him “the best person on the planet,” while his brother said, “The ceremony was beautiful. Adam killed it.”

Travis Kelce and Swift haven’t said much publicly about their wedding since they exchanged vows. Before “New Heights,” Travis Kelce made a brief comment at a Chiefs’ training camp press conference, calling the nuptials “the best night of my life.”
“I wish it could have lasted even longer than it did. It felt like it just happened at a blink of an eye,” he said on “New Heights.”
He also thanked Madison Square Garden for holding the event and meeting their needs.

“We wanted to do it somewhere where we could have a very intimate and genuine setting without a lot of distractions. And we needed it to be a private feel,” he said. “And MSG went above and beyond to give us that.”

title: Where Is Raygun, Australia’s Breakdancer Who Went Viral At The Paris Olympics, Now? She Just Gave an Update
summary: Australian breakdancer Raygun just gave an update on her life two years after her viral Olympics.
story: Raygun has returned to the dance floor.
The Australian breakdancer set social media on fire with her viral performances at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, unleashing a torrent of posts ridiculing her skills.
Two years later, she has shared an update on her life and her Olympic ordeal in the new documentary “Raygun: Breaking Badly,” which is part of Netflix’s “Untold” series.
“I went out there and performed, and I didn’t do as well as I hoped, and then the world freaked out,” Gunn says in the film.
Here is what to know about her story and how she is doing now.
Who Is Raygun?
Raygun is the name used for breaking competitions by Australian Olympian Rachael Gunn.
At the time of the 2024 Olympics, she was a lecturer at Sydney’s Macquarie University with a Ph.D. in Cultural Studies, according to CNBC.
Breaking was introduced as an Olympic sport at the 2024 Games, and Gunn was the women’s qualifier from the Oceania region after winning a competition in Sydney.

She gained notoriety with her two performances in Paris in which she did not earn a single point from the judges across four rounds, losing by a combined 36-0 to two competitors. One particular move in which she mimicked a kangaroo in honor of her native country was turned into a meme.

Social media videos across multiple platforms mocked Gunn’s skills and questioned how she qualified for the Olympics. It brought to life a fear leading up to the Games that she says she shared with her therapist.
“She was like, ‘What’s the worst that could happen?’” Gunn says in the Netflix documentary.
“The worst that could happen is that the whole world could laugh at me,” Gunn says she replied.
“She’s like, ‘Do you think that’s reasonable?’” Gunn says her therapist answered.
An Australian B-girl who goes by Flix says in the Netflix show that she was “offended” and “embarrassed” by Gunn’s performance in Paris.

Another B-girl who goes by Tinylocks, who had previously beaten Gunn in competition, says in the documentary that she told her friends after Gunn’s performance that Gunn was “going to need psychological support.”

Gunn, 38, also shared the strange sensation of realizing she was going viral for all the wrong reasons. Adele was talking about it on stage at one of her concerts, and an NFL player mimicked her kangaroo pose while celebrating an interception.
“I was like, ‘Oh no, I’m a meme,” she says in the documentary. “It was this growing monster. Some of the memes were funny and then the tone started to change.
“It really saddened me to see how many women just decided to hate on me,” she continued. “It was a hot topic talking point to just rip into me.”

She felt like the whole thing might blow over by the end of the Olympics, but it showed no signs of stopping. She shared an Instagram video in August 2024 in which she said all the hate had “been pretty devastating.”
Videos started to circulate alleging she cheated her way into an Olympic berth, which the organizer of the Oceania qualifying event shot down as untrue.
“I was cringe,” she says in the documentary. “I brought shame and embarrassment on the country. Yeah, that was rough.”
She says she felt like her whole life was “crumbling” and she was just trying to get through the day. She also was on antidepressants to deal with the anxiety.
What Happened to Raygun After the Olympics?
Gunn and her husband, Sammy Free, say on the Netflix documentary that they took a trip to the Netherlands for two months after the Olympics to lie low in Europe.
Free is a dancer who introduced Gunn to the art form, but her love for breaking had taken a hard turn after Paris.
“I felt like I was falling into a dark pit,” Gunn says in the film.
She called her parents distraught, and she said her father was crying and asking, “Why you? Out of everyone that was there, why you?”
“I realized my life as I know it is over,” Gunn says.
An Unexpected Lifeline
Gunn reveals in the documentary that she received an emotional lift from Richard Branson, the British billionaire and co-founder of the Virgin Group.
Branson reached out to Gunn after watching her Olympic performance and witnessing the backlash.
“In my opinion, she did something extraordinary,” Branson says in the documentary. “She tried something completely original. She stood out from the crowd.”
He invited Gunn and her husband on a cruise, where she danced for an appreciative crowd.
“The idea was that maybe we could change the narrative a bit,” Branson says.
“That was a lifeline to be honest because that really kept me grounded, and I knew I could get through this,” Gunn says.
Where Is Raygun Now?
Two years removed from her Olympic experience, Gunn has rediscovered her love of dancing.

“I’ve been doing little gradual pushes this whole way, and today my goal is just to dance in front of people and to show what happened after Paris hasn’t defeated me,” she says. “I know for sure I’m never going to stop dancing. Time to be a big brave girl and let’s do this.”
The documentary shows her performing in front of a cheering crowd in Taiwan.
Gunn also reveals that she has left her job in academia.
“I’m excited for what’s next,” she says. “I’m open to where this journey may take me.”

title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Cast 2026: Who’s Competing on Season 35
summary: A new crew of celebrities is gearing up to hit the ballroom floor for Season 35 of “Dancing With the Stars.” Here’s what to know.
story: A new crew of celebrities is gearing up to hit the ballroom floor for Season 35 of “Dancing With the Stars.”
On Sept. 2, the full cast and their partners competing for the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy were announced, with a slew of surprising names.
Returning as co-hosts are Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough, with Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli as judges.

Months ahead of the cast reveal, “Traitors” and “Love Island UK” star Maura Higgins and “Summer House” star Ciara Miller were announced as part of the cast. Last month, it was also announced that Witney Carson, who’s pregnant with baby No. 3, is partnered with Jimmy Kimmel’s sidekick Guillermo Rodriguez.
Mark Ballas who is partnered with Higgins tells TODAY.com the upcoming season “should be a fun one. It seems like a good group.”

Also joining the cast this year as a pro is the winner of “Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro.” The spinoff series, which premiered on July 13, saw 12 dancers compete for a chance to become the next professional on Season 35 of “DWTS.”
